# Balanced 3x2 factorial ANOVA: testing 2-level factor main effect
# Partial eta-squared = 0.06, alpha = 0.05, target power = 0.80

# Design parameters
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.80
partial_eta_sq <- 0.06
numerator_df <- 1  # 2-level factor has 1 DF
factor_a_levels <- 3
factor_b_levels <- 2
total_cells <- factor_a_levels * factor_b_levels

# Convert partial eta-squared to f-squared (effect size)
# Partial eta-squared = f² / (1 + f²)
# Solving for f²: f² = partial_eta_sq / (1 - partial_eta_sq)
f_squared <- partial_eta_sq / (1 - partial_eta_sq)
f <- sqrt(f_squared)

cat("=== Conversion from Partial η² to Effect Size f ===\n")
cat("Partial η²:", partial_eta_sq, "\n")
cat("f²:", f_squared, "\n")
cat("f:", f, "\n\n")

# For a balanced factorial ANOVA with n participants per cell:
# Total N = 6n
# Denominator DF = 6n - 6 (error df in the full model)
# Numerator DF = 1 (main effect of 2-level factor)
# Non-centrality parameter: λ = f × sqrt(n × numerator_df)
#   or equivalently: λ² / (numerator_df) is the expected F ratio × numerator_df

# Using pwr package for F-test power
library(pwr)

# pwr.f2.test uses f² (effect size squared) and u (numerator df), v (denominator df)
# But we need to be careful: pwr package uses Cohen's f, not f²

# Let's use the direct approach with non-centrality parameter
# Non-centrality parameter λ = f × sqrt(numerator_df × n)
# Where n is per-cell sample size

# We'll search for minimum n that achieves target power
candidate_ns <- seq(1, 200, by = 1)
achieved_powers <- numeric(length(candidate_ns))

for (i in seq_along(candidate_ns)) {
  n_per_cell <- candidate_ns[i]
  # Non-centrality parameter
  lambda <- f * sqrt(numerator_df * n_per_cell)
  # Denominator DF
  denominator_df <- total_cells * n_per_cell - total_cells
  # Power calculation using non-central F distribution
  critical_f <- qf(1 - alpha, numerator_df, denominator_df)
  achieved_powers[i] <- 1 - pf(critical_f, numerator_df, denominator_df, ncp = lambda)
}

# Find minimum n with power >= 0.80
valid_idx <- which(achieved_powers >= target_power)
if (length(valid_idx) > 0) {
  min_idx <- min(valid_idx)
  n_min <- candidate_ns[min_idx]
  power_at_min <- achieved_powers[min_idx]
  
  # Also show the preceding n
  if (min_idx > 1) {
    n_preceding <- candidate_ns[min_idx - 1]
    power_at_preceding <- achieved_powers[min_idx - 1]
  } else {
    n_preceding <- NA
    power_at_preceding <- NA
  }
} else {
  cat("ERROR: Could not achieve target power within search range\n")
  n_min <- NA
  power_at_min <- NA
  n_preceding <- NA
  power_at_preceding <- NA
}

cat("\n=== Sample Size Calculation Results ===\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("Significance level (alpha):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Numerator DF:", numerator_df, "\n")
cat("Factor A levels:", factor_a_levels, "\n")
cat("Factor B levels:", factor_b_levels, "\n")
cat("Total cells:", total_cells, "\n\n")

if (!is.na(n_preceding)) {
  cat("Preceding design (n-1):\n")
  cat("  Participants per cell:", n_preceding, "\n")
  cat("  Total participants:", n_preceding * total_cells, "\n")
  cat("  Denominator DF:", total_cells * n_preceding - total_cells, "\n")
  cat("  Achieved power:", round(power_at_preceding, 4), "\n\n")
}

cat("Minimum design meeting target:\n")
cat("  Participants per cell:", n_min, "\n")
cat("  Total participants:", n_min * total_cells, "\n")
cat("  Denominator DF:", total_cells * n_min - total_cells, "\n")
cat("  Achieved power:", round(power_at_min, 4), "\n")

# Prepare JSON output
result_df <- data.frame(
  metric = "sample_size",
  value = n_min,
  unit = "participants_per_cell"
)

cat("\n=== Verification ===\n")
cat("Non-centrality parameter λ at n =", n_min, ":\n")
lambda_final <- f * sqrt(numerator_df * n_min)
cat("  λ =", lambda_final, "\n")
denominator_df_final <- total_cells * n_min - total_cells
critical_f_final <- qf(1 - alpha, numerator_df, denominator_df_final)
cat("  Critical F-value:", critical_f_final, "\n")
cat("  Denominator DF:", denominator_df_final, "\n")
power_check <- 1 - pf(critical_f_final, numerator_df, denominator_df_final, ncp = lambda_final)
cat("  Verified power:", power_check, "\n")

# JSON output
library(jsonlite)
output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = n_min,
      unit = "participants_per_cell"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "achieved_power",
      value = round(power_at_min, 6),
      unit = "probability"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "total_participants",
      value = n_min * total_cells,
      unit = "participants_total"
    )
  )
)

if (!is.na(power_at_preceding)) {
  output$results[[4]] <- list(
    metric = "power_at_preceding_design",
    value = round(power_at_preceding, 6),
    unit = "probability"
  )
  output$results[[5]] <- list(
    metric = "preceding_sample_size",
    value = n_preceding,
    unit = "participants_per_cell"
  )
}

cat("\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

# Balanced 3x2 factorial ANOVA: testing 2-level factor main effect
# Partial eta-squared = 0.06, alpha = 0.05, target power = 0.80

# Design parameters
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.80
partial_eta_sq <- 0.06
numerator_df <- 1  # 2-level factor has 1 DF
factor_a_levels <- 3
factor_b_levels <- 2
total_cells <- factor_a_levels * factor_b_levels

# Convert partial eta-squared to f-squared (effect size)
# Partial eta-squared = f² / (1 + f²)
# Solving for f²: f² = partial_eta_sq / (1 - partial_eta_sq)
f_squared <- partial_eta_sq / (1 - partial_eta_sq)
f <- sqrt(f_squared)

cat("=== Conversion from Partial η² to Effect Size f ===\n")
cat("Partial η²:", partial_eta_sq, "\n")
cat("f²:", f_squared, "\n")
cat("f:", f, "\n\n")

# For a balanced factorial ANOVA with n participants per cell:
# Total N = 6n
# Denominator DF = 6n - 6 (error df in the full model)
# Numerator DF = 1 (main effect of 2-level factor)
# Non-centrality parameter: λ = f × sqrt(n × numerator_df)
#   or equivalently: λ² / (numerator_df) is the expected F ratio × numerator_df

# Using pwr package for F-test power
library(pwr)

# pwr.f2.test uses f² (effect size squared) and u (numerator df), v (denominator df)
# But we need to be careful: pwr package uses Cohen's f, not f²

# Let's use the direct approach with non-centrality parameter
# Non-centrality parameter λ = f × sqrt(numerator_df × n)
# Where n is per-cell sample size

# We'll search for minimum n that achieves target power
candidate_ns <- seq(1, 200, by = 1)
achieved_powers <- numeric(length(candidate_ns))

for (i in seq_along(candidate_ns)) {
  n_per_cell <- candidate_ns[i]
  # Non-centrality parameter
  lambda <- f * sqrt(numerator_df * n_per_cell)
  # Denominator DF
  denominator_df <- total_cells * n_per_cell - total_cells
  # Power calculation using non-central F distribution
  critical_f <- qf(1 - alpha, numerator_df, denominator_df)
  achieved_powers[i] <- 1 - pf(critical_f, numerator_df, denominator_df, ncp = lambda)
}

# Find minimum n with power >= 0.80
valid_idx <- which(achieved_powers >= target_power)
if (length(valid_idx) > 0) {
  min_idx <- min(valid_idx)
  n_min <- candidate_ns[min_idx]
  power_at_min <- achieved_powers[min_idx]
  
  # Also show the preceding n
  if (min_idx > 1) {
    n_preceding <- candidate_ns[min_idx - 1]
    power_at_preceding <- achieved_powers[min_idx - 1]
  } else {
    n_preceding <- NA
    power_at_preceding <- NA
  }
} else {
  cat("ERROR: Could not achieve target power within search range\n")
  n_min <- NA
  power_at_min <- NA
  n_preceding <- NA
  power_at_preceding <- NA
}

cat("\n=== Sample Size Calculation Results ===\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("Significance level (alpha):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Numerator DF:", numerator_df, "\n")
cat("Factor A levels:", factor_a_levels, "\n")
cat("Factor B levels:", factor_b_levels, "\n")
cat("Total cells:", total_cells, "\n\n")

if (!is.na(n_preceding)) {
  cat("Preceding design (n-1):\n")
  cat("  Participants per cell:", n_preceding, "\n")
  cat("  Total participants:", n_preceding * total_cells, "\n")
  cat("  Denominator DF:", total_cells * n_preceding - total_cells, "\n")
  cat("  Achieved power:", round(power_at_preceding, 4), "\n\n")
}

cat("Minimum design meeting target:\n")
cat("  Participants per cell:", n_min, "\n")
cat("  Total participants:", n_min * total_cells, "\n")
cat("  Denominator DF:", total_cells * n_min - total_cells, "\n")
cat("  Achieved power:", round(power_at_min, 4), "\n")

# Prepare JSON output
result_df <- data.frame(
  metric = "sample_size",
  value = n_min,
  unit = "participants_per_cell"
)

cat("\n=== Verification ===\n")
cat("Non-centrality parameter λ at n =", n_min, ":\n")
lambda_final <- f * sqrt(numerator_df * n_min)
cat("  λ =", lambda_final, "\n")
denominator_df_final <- total_cells * n_min - total_cells
critical_f_final <- qf(1 - alpha, numerator_df, denominator_df_final)
cat("  Critical F-value:", critical_f_final, "\n")
cat("  Denominator DF:", denominator_df_final, "\n")
power_check <- 1 - pf(critical_f_final, numerator_df, denominator_df_final, ncp = lambda_final)
cat("  Verified power:", power_check, "\n")

# JSON output
library(jsonlite)
output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = n_min,
      unit = "participants_per_cell"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "achieved_power",
      value = round(power_at_min, 6),
      unit = "probability"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "total_participants",
      value = n_min * total_cells,
      unit = "participants_total"

# Extended search for minimum sample size per cell
# Balanced 3x2 factorial ANOVA: testing 2-level factor main effect
# Partial eta-squared = 0.06, alpha = 0.05, target power = 0.80

# Design parameters
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.80
partial_eta_sq <- 0.06
numerator_df <- 1  # 2-level factor has 1 DF
factor_a_levels <- 3
factor_b_levels <- 2
total_cells <- factor_a_levels * factor_b_levels

# Convert partial eta-squared to f (Cohen's effect size)
# Partial eta-squared = f² / (1 + f²)
# Solving for f²: f² = partial_eta_sq / (1 - partial_eta_sq)
f_squared <- partial_eta_sq / (1 - partial_eta_sq)
f <- sqrt(f_squared)

cat("=== Conversion from Partial η² to Effect Size f ===\n")
cat("Partial η²:", partial_eta_sq, "\n")
cat("f²:", f_squared, "\n")
cat("f:", f, "\n\n")

# Extended search range
candidate_ns <- seq(1, 1000, by = 1)
achieved_powers <- numeric(length(candidate_ns))

for (i in seq_along(candidate_ns)) {
  n_per_cell <- candidate_ns[i]
  # Non-centrality parameter: λ = f × sqrt(numerator_df × n)
  lambda <- f * sqrt(numerator_df * n_per_cell)
  # Denominator DF in the full model with balanced design
  denominator_df <- total_cells * n_per_cell - total_cells
  # Critical F-value at alpha level
  critical_f <- qf(1 - alpha, numerator_df, denominator_df)
  # Power: probability that F exceeds critical value under non-null
  achieved_powers[i] <- 1 - pf(critical_f, numerator_df, denominator_df, ncp = lambda)
}

# Find minimum n with power >= 0.80
valid_idx <- which(achieved_powers >= target_power)

if (length(valid_idx) > 0) {
  min_idx <- min(valid_idx)
  n_min <- candidate_ns[min_idx]
  power_at_min <- achieved_powers[min_idx]
  
  # Also show the preceding n
  if (min_idx > 1) {
    n_preceding <- candidate_ns[min_idx - 1]
    power_at_preceding <- achieved_powers[min_idx - 1]
  } else {
    n_preceding <- NA
    power_at_preceding <- NA
  }
  
  cat("\n=== Sample Size Calculation Results ===\n")
  cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
  cat("Significance level (alpha):", alpha, "\n")
  cat("Numerator DF:", numerator_df, "\n")
  cat("Effect size f:", round(f, 6), "\n")
  cat("Effect size f²:", round(f_squared, 6), "\n")
  cat("Partial η²:", partial_eta_sq, "\n")
  cat("Design: 3 × 2 factorial (", total_cells, "cells)\n\n")
  
  if (!is.na(n_preceding)) {
    cat("Preceding design (n-1):\n")
    cat("  Participants per cell:", n_preceding, "\n")
    cat("  Total participants:", n_preceding * total_cells, "\n")
    cat("  Denominator DF:", total_cells * n_preceding - total_cells, "\n")
    cat("  Achieved power:", round(power_at_preceding, 6), "\n\n")
  }
  
  cat("Minimum design meeting target:\n")
  cat("  Participants per cell:", n_min, "\n")
  cat("  Total participants:", n_min * total_cells, "\n")
  cat("  Denominator DF:", total_cells * n_min - total_cells, "\n")
  cat("  Achieved power:", round(power_at_min, 6), "\n\n")
  
  # Verification
  cat("=== Verification at n =", n_min, "===\n")
  lambda_final <- f * sqrt(numerator_df * n_min)
  denominator_df_final <- total_cells * n_min - total_cells
  critical_f_final <- qf(1 - alpha, numerator_df, denominator_df_final)
  power_check <- 1 - pf(critical_f_final, numerator_df, denominator_df_final, ncp = lambda_final)
  
  cat("Non-centrality parameter λ:", lambda_final, "\n")
  cat("Critical F-value (α =", alpha, "):", critical_f_final, "\n")
  cat("Numerator DF:", numerator_df, "\n")
  cat("Denominator DF:", denominator_df_final, "\n")
  cat("Verified power:", power_check, "\n")
  
} else {
  cat("ERROR: Could not achieve target power within extended search range (up to n=1000)\n")
}

# JSON output with all relevant results
library(jsonlite)

output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = n_min,
      unit = "participants_per_cell"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "achieved_power",
      value = round(power_at_min, 6),
      unit = "probability"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "total_participants",
      value = n_min * total_cells,
      unit = "participants_total"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "preceding_sample_size",
      value = n_preceding,
      unit = "participants_per_cell"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "power_at_preceding_design",
      value = round(power_at_preceding, 6),
      unit = "probability"
    )
  )
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

# Evidence e1; success=true

# Balanced 3x2 factorial ANOVA: testing 2-level factor main effect
# Partial eta-squared = 0.06, alpha = 0.05, target power = 0.80

# Design parameters
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.80
partial_eta_sq <- 0.06
numerator_df <- 1  # 2-level factor has 1 DF
factor_a_levels <- 3
factor_b_levels <- 2
total_cells <- factor_a_levels * factor_b_levels

# Convert partial eta-squared to f-squared (effect size)
# Partial eta-squared = f² / (1 + f²)
# Solving for f²: f² = partial_eta_sq / (1 - partial_eta_sq)
f_squared <- partial_eta_sq / (1 - partial_eta_sq)
f <- sqrt(f_squared)

cat("=== Conversion from Partial η² to Effect Size f ===\n")
cat("Partial η²:", partial_eta_sq, "\n")
cat("f²:", f_squared, "\n")
cat("f:", f, "\n\n")

# For a balanced factorial ANOVA with n participants per cell:
# Total N = 6n
# Denominator DF = 6n - 6 (error df in the full model)
# Numerator DF = 1 (main effect of 2-level factor)
# Non-centrality parameter: λ = f × sqrt(n × numerator_df)
#   or equivalently: λ² / (numerator_df) is the expected F ratio × numerator_df

# Using pwr package for F-test power
library(pwr)

# pwr.f2.test uses f² (effect size squared) and u (numerator df), v (denominator df)
# But we need to be careful: pwr package uses Cohen's f, not f²

# Let's use the direct approach with non-centrality parameter
# Non-centrality parameter λ = f × sqrt(numerator_df × n)
# Where n is per-cell sample size

# We'll search for minimum n that achieves target power
candidate_ns <- seq(1, 200, by = 1)
achieved_powers <- numeric(length(candidate_ns))

for (i in seq_along(candidate_ns)) {
  n_per_cell <- candidate_ns[i]
  # Non-centrality parameter
  lambda <- f * sqrt(numerator_df * n_per_cell)
  # Denominator DF
  denominator_df <- total_cells * n_per_cell - total_cells
  # Power calculation using non-central F distribution
  critical_f <- qf(1 - alpha, numerator_df, denominator_df)
  achieved_powers[i] <- 1 - pf(critical_f, numerator_df, denominator_df, ncp = lambda)
}

# Find minimum n with power >= 0.80
valid_idx <- which(achieved_powers >= target_power)
if (length(valid_idx) > 0) {
  min_idx <- min(valid_idx)
  n_min <- candidate_ns[min_idx]
  power_at_min <- achieved_powers[min_idx]
  
  # Also show the preceding n
  if (min_idx > 1) {
    n_preceding <- candidate_ns[min_idx - 1]
    power_at_preceding <- achieved_powers[min_idx - 1]
  } else {
    n_preceding <- NA
    power_at_preceding <- NA
  }
} else {
  cat("ERROR: Could not achieve target power within search range\n")
  n_min <- NA
  power_at_min <- NA
  n_preceding <- NA
  power_at_preceding <- NA
}

cat("\n=== Sample Size Calculation Results ===\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("Significance level (alpha):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Numerator DF:", numerator_df, "\n")
cat("Factor A levels:", factor_a_levels, "\n")
cat("Factor B levels:", factor_b_levels, "\n")
cat("Total cells:", total_cells, "\n\n")

if (!is.na(n_preceding)) {
  cat("Preceding design (n-1):\n")
  cat("  Participants per cell:", n_preceding, "\n")
  cat("  Total participants:", n_preceding * total_cells, "\n")
  cat("  Denominator DF:", total_cells * n_preceding - total_cells, "\n")
  cat("  Achieved power:", round(power_at_preceding, 4), "\n\n")
}

cat("Minimum design meeting target:\n")
cat("  Participants per cell:", n_min, "\n")
cat("  Total participants:", n_min * total_cells, "\n")
cat("  Denominator DF:", total_cells * n_min - total_cells, "\n")
cat("  Achieved power:", round(power_at_min, 4), "\n")

# Prepare JSON output
result_df <- data.frame(
  metric = "sample_size",
  value = n_min,
  unit = "participants_per_cell"
)

cat("\n=== Verification ===\n")
cat("Non-centrality parameter λ at n =", n_min, ":\n")
lambda_final <- f * sqrt(numerator_df * n_min)
cat("  λ =", lambda_final, "\n")
denominator_df_final <- total_cells * n_min - total_cells
critical_f_final <- qf(1 - alpha, numerator_df, denominator_df_final)
cat("  Critical F-value:", critical_f_final, "\n")
cat("  Denominator DF:", denominator_df_final, "\n")
power_check <- 1 - pf(critical_f_final, numerator_df, denominator_df_final, ncp = lambda_final)
cat("  Verified power:", power_check, "\n")

# JSON output
library(jsonlite)
output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = n_min,
      unit = "participants_per_cell"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "achieved_power",
      value = round(power_at_min, 6),
      unit = "probability"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "total_participants",
      value = n_min * total_cells,
      unit = "participants_total"
    )
  )
)

if (!is.na(power_at_preceding)) {
  output$results[[4]] <- list(
    metric = "power_at_preceding_design",
    value = round(power_at_preceding, 6),
    unit = "probability"
  )
  output$results[[5]] <- list(
    metric = "preceding_sample_size",
    value = n_preceding,
    unit = "participants_per_cell"
  )
}

cat("\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

plan.estimand: Mean difference between two groups, estimated from participant-level averages in a random-intercept Gaussian repeated-measures design
plan.hypothesis: H0: mean group difference = 0 vs H1: mean group difference ≠ 0
assumptions: Random-intercept Gaussian model with exchangeable correlation within participants
Marginal mean structure: E[Y_{ij}] = μ + δ*group_i, where δ = 0.45
Marginal variance: Var(Y_{ij}) = 1 (constant across groups and time)
Intraclass correlation ρ = 0.4 (constant within each participant)
Analysis method: two-sided pooled two-sample t-test on participant-level means (averaging m=4 observations per participant)
Significance level α = 0.05
Equal allocation: n per group
No missing data
Normality of participant-averaged outcomes
scientific_notes: The marginal variance decomposition in a random-intercept model: Var(Y_{ij}) = τ² + σ² = 1, where τ² is the random-intercept variance and σ² is the within-participant error variance. The intraclass correlation is ρ = τ²/(τ²+σ²) = 0.4, implying τ² = 0.4 and σ² = 0.6.
When analyzing participant-level averages Ȳ_i = (1/m)∑_{j=1}^{m} Y_{ij}, the variance of each average is Var(Ȳ_i) = [τ² + σ²/m] = [0.4 + 0.6/4] = 0.4 + 0.15 = 0.55.
The effective standard deviation of participant means is √0.55 ≈ 0.7416, pooled across groups.
The t-test compares two group means with pooled standard error SE = √0.55 × √(2/n), where n is the per-group sample size.
Non-centrality parameter for the t-test: Δ/SE = 0.45 / √(1.1/n) = 0.45√(n/1.1).
Power calculation inverts the non-central t distribution with α=0.05 (two-sided critical value ≈1.96 for large n) and df=2n-2 to find the minimum n achieving target power = 0.90.

# Two-group random-intercept repeated-measures study power calculation
# Analysis method: participant-level averages with pooled t-test

# Study parameters
m <- 4           # observations per participant
marginal_sd <- 1 # marginal SD
rho <- 0.4       # intraclass correlation (ICC)
delta <- 0.45    # group mean difference
alpha <- 0.05    # significance level (two-sided)
target_power <- 0.90

# Derived variance parameters
# Var(Y_ij) = tau^2 + sigma^2 = 1
# rho = tau^2 / (tau^2 + sigma^2) = 0.4
tau_sq <- rho           # random-intercept variance
sigma_sq <- 1 - rho     # within-participant error variance

cat("=== Variance Decomposition ===\n")
cat("Marginal variance: Var(Y_ij) =", marginal_sd^2, "\n")
cat("Random-intercept variance (tau^2):", tau_sq, "\n")
cat("Within-participant error variance (sigma^2):", sigma_sq, "\n")
cat("ICC = tau^2 / (tau^2 + sigma^2) =", tau_sq / (tau_sq + sigma_sq), "\n\n")

# Variance of participant-level averages
# Var(Y_bar_i) = tau^2 + sigma^2/m
var_participant_mean <- tau_sq + sigma_sq / m
sd_participant_mean <- sqrt(var_participant_mean)

cat("=== Participant-Level Average Distribution ===\n")
cat("Var(Y_bar_i) = tau^2 + sigma^2/m =", tau_sq, "+", sigma_sq/m, "=", var_participant_mean, "\n")
cat("SD(Y_bar_i) =", sd_participant_mean, "\n\n")

# Pooled standard error for comparing two groups
# SE = sd_participant_mean * sqrt(2/n) = sqrt(var_participant_mean * 2/n)
# t-statistic: t = delta / SE = delta / sqrt(var_participant_mean * 2/n)
# Non-centrality: lambda = delta / SE for fixed n

# Function to calculate power for a given sample size per group
calc_power <- function(n, delta, var_pm, alpha = 0.05) {
  df <- 2 * n - 2
  # Standard error: SE = sqrt(var_pm * 2/n)
  se <- sqrt(var_pm * 2 / n)
  # Non-centrality parameter
  ncp <- delta / se
  # Critical value (two-sided)
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = df)
  # Power: P(|t| > t_crit | H1)
  power <- pt(-t_crit, df = df, ncp = ncp) + pt(t_crit, df = df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE)
  return(power)
}

# Search for minimum sample size achieving target power
# Start with a reasonable range
n_search <- seq(1, 100)
powers <- sapply(n_search, function(n) calc_power(n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha))

# Find minimum n where power >= target_power
min_n <- min(n_search[powers >= target_power])

cat("=== Power Calculation Results ===\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("Significance level (two-sided):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Group mean difference:", delta, "\n")
cat("Participant-level SD:", sd_participant_mean, "\n\n")

# Display powers around the minimum
display_range <- max(1, min_n - 2) : (min_n + 2)
for (n in display_range) {
  pw <- calc_power(n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha)
  se <- sqrt(var_participant_mean * 2 / n)
  ncp <- delta / se
  df <- 2 * n - 2
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = df)
  cat(sprintf("n = %3d (df = %4d): SE = %.6f, ncp = %.6f, power = %.6f\n", 
              n, df, se, ncp, pw))
}

cat("\n=== ANSWER ===\n")
cat("Minimum participants per group (integer):", min_n, "\n")
cat("Achieved power at n =", min_n, ":", calc_power(min_n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha), "\n")
cat("Power at n =", min_n - 1, ":", calc_power(min_n - 1, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha), "\n")

# Prepare JSON output
results <- list(
  metric = "sample_size",
  value = min_n,
  unit = "participants_per_group"
)

# Include additional verification metrics
achieved_power <- calc_power(min_n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha)
preceding_power <- calc_power(min_n - 1, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha)

cat("\n=== JSON Result ===\n")
result_json <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = min_n, unit = "participants_per_group"),
    list(metric = "achieved_power", value = achieved_power, unit = "probability"),
    list(metric = "preceding_sample_size", value = min_n - 1, unit = "participants_per_group"),
    list(metric = "power_at_preceding_n", value = preceding_power, unit = "probability")
  )
)

library(jsonlite)
cat(toJSON(result_json, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

power_calc <- function(n) {
  df <- 2*n - 2
  se <- sqrt(var_ybar * 2/n)
  lambda <- delta / se
  
  # Critical value for two-sided test
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df)
  
  # Power = P(|t| > t_crit | H1 with ncp = lambda)
  # This is P(t > t_crit) + P(t < -t_crit) under non-central t with ncp = lambda
  power <- pt(t_crit, df, ncp = lambda, lower.tail = FALSE) + 
           pt(-t_crit, df, ncp = lambda, lower.tail = TRUE)
  
  return(list(n = n, df = df, se = se, lambda = lambda, t_crit = t_crit, power = power))
}

# Focus on: (1) variance formula for participant averages, (2) test specification

cat("=== DETAILED MODEL VERIFICATION ===\n\n")

# Parameters
m <- 4
rho <- 0.4
sigma2_marginal <- 1  # marginal variance = 1

# From ICC definition: rho = tau^2 / (tau^2 + sigma^2) where tau^2 + sigma^2 = sigma2_marginal
tau_sq <- rho * sigma2_marginal
sigma_sq <- (1 - rho) * sigma2_marginal

cat("1. VARIANCE DECOMPOSITION\n")
cat("   Random-intercept model: Y_ij = mu_i + epsilon_ij\n")
cat("   where mu_i ~ N(0, tau^2) and epsilon_ij ~ N(0, sigma^2)\n")
cat("   ICC = tau^2 / (tau^2 + sigma^2) =", rho, "\n")
cat("   Given marginal variance = 1, we solve:\n")
cat("   tau^2 + sigma^2 = 1 and tau^2/(tau^2+sigma^2) = 0.4\n")
cat("   => tau^2 =", tau_sq, "and sigma^2 =", sigma_sq, "\n\n")

# Variance of individual observation
var_individual <- tau_sq + sigma_sq
cat("2. INDIVIDUAL-LEVEL VARIANCE\n")
cat("   Var(Y_ij) = tau^2 + sigma^2 =", var_individual, "\n\n")

# Variance of participant average
var_avg <- tau_sq + sigma_sq / m
sd_avg <- sqrt(var_avg)

cat("3. PARTICIPANT-AVERAGE VARIANCE\n")
cat("   When computing Ybar_i = (1/m) * sum_j Y_ij:\n")
cat("   Var(Ybar_i) = Var(mu_i + (1/m)*sum_j epsilon_ij)\n")
cat("              = Var(mu_i) + Var((1/m)*sum_j epsilon_ij)\n")
cat("              = tau^2 + (1/m^2) * m * sigma^2   [independent random effects]\n")
cat("              = tau^2 + sigma^2/m\n")
cat("              =", tau_sq, "+", sigma_sq/m, "\n")
cat("              =", var_avg, "\n")
cat("   SD(Ybar_i) =", sd_avg, "\n\n")

# Effective correlation structure comment
cat("4. CORRELATION STRUCTURE\n")
cat("   Within-participant correlation (exchangeable):\n")
cat("   Cov(Y_ij, Y_ij') = tau^2 for j ≠ j'\n")
cat("   Correlation = tau^2 / Var(Y_ij) = tau^2 / 1 =", tau_sq, "\n")
cat("   This matches the specified ICC = 0.4 ✓\n\n")

# Two-sample t-test specification
cat("5. TWO-SAMPLE T-TEST SPECIFICATION\n")
cat("   H0: E(Ybar_1) = E(Ybar_2), vs H1: E(Ybar_1) - E(Ybar_2) = 0.45\n")
cat("   Assumption: Ybar_i ~ N(mu_group, Var(Ybar_i)) independently\n")
cat("   Test statistic: t = (Ybar_1 - Ybar_2) / sqrt(s_p^2 * (2/n))\n")
cat("   where s_p^2 is the pooled sample variance, approximately = Var(Ybar_i)\n")
cat("   Under H0: t ~ t_{2n-2}\n")
cat("   Under H1: t ~ t_{2n-2}(lambda) with lambda = 0.45 / sqrt(Var(Ybar_i)*2/n)\n\n")

# Verification with specific n value
n <- 59
df <- 2*n - 2
se <- sqrt(var_avg * 2/n)
ncp <- 0.45 / se
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df)  # two-sided, alpha=0.05

cat("6. POWER CALCULATION FOR n=59\n")
cat("   df =", df, "\n")
cat("   SE = sqrt(", var_avg, "* 2/59) =", se, "\n")
cat("   Non-centrality (lambda) = 0.45 /", se, "=", ncp, "\n")
cat("   t_critical (two-sided, alpha=0.05) =", t_crit, "\n")
cat("   Power = P(|t| > t_crit | H1) under t_{116}(lambda=", ncp, ")\n")

power_left <- pt(-t_crit, df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = TRUE)
power_right <- pt(t_crit, df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE)
power_total <- power_left + power_right

cat("        = P(t < -", t_crit, ") + P(t >", t_crit, ")\n")
cat("        = ", power_left, "+", power_right, "\n")
cat("        = ", power_total, "\n")
cat("   Target met (>= 0.90)? ", power_total >= 0.90, "\n\n")

# Formula check: alternative calculation
cat("7. FORMULA CONSISTENCY CHECK\n")
cat("   Non-central t power formula:\n")
cat("   Power = pt(-t_crit, df, ncp) + pt(t_crit, df, ncp, lower.tail=F)\n")
cat("   For n=59:\n")

# Using power calculation from non-central t
power_via_formula <- pt(-t_crit, df, ncp = ncp) + pt(t_crit, df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE)
cat("   Direct calculation:", power_via_formula, "\n")

# Verify this matches previous result

  df <- 2*n - 2

  cat(sprintf("   n=%2d: power = %.6f%s\n", n, p, marker))
}

plan.estimand: Mean difference between two groups, estimated from participant-level averages in a random-intercept Gaussian repeated-measures design
plan.hypothesis: H0: mean group difference = 0 vs H1: mean group difference ≠ 0
assumptions: Random-intercept Gaussian model with exchangeable correlation within participants
Marginal mean structure: E[Y_{ij}] = μ + δ*group_i, where δ = 0.45
Marginal variance: Var(Y_{ij}) = 1 (constant across groups and time)
Intraclass correlation ρ = 0.4 (constant within each participant)
Analysis method: two-sided pooled two-sample t-test on participant-level means (averaging m=4 observations per participant)
Significance level α = 0.05
Equal allocation: n per group
No missing data
Normality of participant-averaged outcomes
scientific_notes: The marginal variance decomposition in a random-intercept model: Var(Y_{ij}) = τ² + σ² = 1, where τ² is the random-intercept variance and σ² is the within-participant error variance. The intraclass correlation is ρ = τ²/(τ²+σ²) = 0.4, implying τ² = 0.4 and σ² = 0.6.
When analyzing participant-level averages Ȳ_i = (1/m)∑_{j=1}^{m} Y_{ij}, the variance of each average is Var(Ȳ_i) = [τ² + σ²/m] = [0.4 + 0.6/4] = 0.4 + 0.15 = 0.55.
The effective standard deviation of participant means is √0.55 ≈ 0.7416, pooled across groups.
The t-test compares two group means with pooled standard error SE = √0.55 × √(2/n), where n is the per-group sample size.
Non-centrality parameter for the t-test: Δ/SE = 0.45 / √(1.1/n) = 0.45√(n/1.1).
Power calculation inverts the non-central t distribution with α=0.05 (two-sided critical value ≈1.96 for large n) and df=2n-2 to find the minimum n achieving target power = 0.90.

# Two-group random-intercept repeated-measures study power calculation
# Analysis method: participant-level averages with pooled t-test

# Study parameters
m <- 4           # observations per participant
marginal_sd <- 1 # marginal SD
rho <- 0.4       # intraclass correlation (ICC)
delta <- 0.45    # group mean difference
alpha <- 0.05    # significance level (two-sided)
target_power <- 0.90

# Derived variance parameters
# Var(Y_ij) = tau^2 + sigma^2 = 1
# rho = tau^2 / (tau^2 + sigma^2) = 0.4
tau_sq <- rho           # random-intercept variance
sigma_sq <- 1 - rho     # within-participant error variance

cat("=== Variance Decomposition ===\n")
cat("Marginal variance: Var(Y_ij) =", marginal_sd^2, "\n")
cat("Random-intercept variance (tau^2):", tau_sq, "\n")
cat("Within-participant error variance (sigma^2):", sigma_sq, "\n")
cat("ICC = tau^2 / (tau^2 + sigma^2) =", tau_sq / (tau_sq + sigma_sq), "\n\n")

# Variance of participant-level averages
# Var(Y_bar_i) = tau^2 + sigma^2/m
var_participant_mean <- tau_sq + sigma_sq / m
sd_participant_mean <- sqrt(var_participant_mean)

cat("=== Participant-Level Average Distribution ===\n")
cat("Var(Y_bar_i) = tau^2 + sigma^2/m =", tau_sq, "+", sigma_sq/m, "=", var_participant_mean, "\n")
cat("SD(Y_bar_i) =", sd_participant_mean, "\n\n")

# Pooled standard error for comparing two groups
# SE = sd_participant_mean * sqrt(2/n) = sqrt(var_participant_mean * 2/n)
# t-statistic: t = delta / SE = delta / sqrt(var_participant_mean * 2/n)
# Non-centrality: lambda = delta / SE for fixed n

# Function to calculate power for a given sample size per group
calc_power <- function(n, delta, var_pm, alpha = 0.05) {
  df <- 2 * n - 2
  # Standard error: SE = sqrt(var_pm * 2/n)
  se <- sqrt(var_pm * 2 / n)
  # Non-centrality parameter
  ncp <- delta / se
  # Critical value (two-sided)
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = df)
  # Power: P(|t| > t_crit | H1)
  power <- pt(-t_crit, df = df, ncp = ncp) + pt(t_crit, df = df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE)
  return(power)
}

# Search for minimum sample size achieving target power
# Start with a reasonable range
n_search <- seq(1, 100)
powers <- sapply(n_search, function(n) calc_power(n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha))

# Find minimum n where power >= target_power
min_n <- min(n_search[powers >= target_power])

cat("=== Power Calculation Results ===\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("Significance level (two-sided):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Group mean difference:", delta, "\n")
cat("Participant-level SD:", sd_participant_mean, "\n\n")

# Display powers around the minimum
display_range <- max(1, min_n - 2) : (min_n + 2)
for (n in display_range) {
  pw <- calc_power(n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha)
  se <- sqrt(var_participant_mean * 2 / n)
  ncp <- delta / se
  df <- 2 * n - 2
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = df)
  cat(sprintf("n = %3d (df = %4d): SE = %.6f, ncp = %.6f, power = %.6f\n", 
              n, df, se, ncp, pw))
}

cat("\n=== ANSWER ===\n")
cat("Minimum participants per group (integer):", min_n, "\n")
cat("Achieved power at n =", min_n, ":", calc_power(min_n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha), "\n")
cat("Power at n =", min_n - 1, ":", calc_power(min_n - 1, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha), "\n")

# Prepare JSON output
results <- list(
  metric = "sample_size",
  value = min_n,
  unit = "participants_per_group"

# Two-group random-intercept repeated-measures study power calculation
# Analysis method: participant-level averages with pooled t-test

# Study parameters
m <- 4           # observations per participant
marginal_sd <- 1 # marginal SD
rho <- 0.4       # intraclass correlation (ICC)
delta <- 0.45    # group mean difference
alpha <- 0.05    # significance level (two-sided)
target_power <- 0.90

# Derived variance parameters
tau_sq <- rho           # random-intercept variance
sigma_sq <- 1 - rho     # within-participant error variance

# Variance of participant-level averages
var_participant_mean <- tau_sq + sigma_sq / m
sd_participant_mean <- sqrt(var_participant_mean)

cat("=== Variance Decomposition ===\n")
cat("Random-intercept variance (tau^2):", tau_sq, "\n")
cat("Within-participant error variance (sigma^2):", sigma_sq, "\n")
cat("Var(Y_bar_i) = tau^2 + sigma^2/m =", var_participant_mean, "\n")
cat("SD(Y_bar_i) =", sd_participant_mean, "\n\n")

# Function to calculate power for a given sample size per group
calc_power <- function(n, delta, var_pm, alpha = 0.05) {
  if (n < 1) return(NA)
  df <- 2 * n - 2
  # Standard error: SE = sqrt(var_pm * 2/n)
  se <- sqrt(var_pm * 2 / n)
  # Non-centrality parameter
  ncp <- delta / se
  # Critical value (two-sided)
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = df)
  # Power: P(|t| > t_crit | H1)
  power <- pt(-t_crit, df = df, ncp = ncp) + pt(t_crit, df = df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE)
  return(power)
}

# Expanded search range
n_search <- seq(1, 200)
powers <- sapply(n_search, function(n) calc_power(n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha))

# Check if any power >= target
if (sum(powers >= target_power, na.rm = TRUE) == 0) {
  cat("Warning: No sample size in range [1, 200] achieves target power of", target_power, "\n")
  cat("Maximum power observed: ", max(powers, na.rm = TRUE), "at n =", n_search[which.max(powers)], "\n\n")
}

# Find minimum n where power >= target_power
idx_target <- which(powers >= target_power)
if (length(idx_target) > 0) {
  min_n <- n_search[idx_target[1]]
} else {
  # Extend search further if needed
  n_search_extended <- seq(1, 500)
  powers_extended <- sapply(n_search_extended, function(n) calc_power(n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha))
  idx_target <- which(powers_extended >= target_power)
  if (length(idx_target) > 0) {
    min_n <- n_search_extended[idx_target[1]]
    n_search <- n_search_extended
    powers <- powers_extended
  } else {
    stop("Cannot achieve target power with reasonable sample sizes")
  }
}

cat("=== Power Calculation Results ===\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("Significance level (two-sided):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Group mean difference:", delta, "\n")
cat("Participant-level SD:", sd_participant_mean, "\n\n")

# Display powers around the minimum
display_start <- max(1, min_n - 3)
display_end <- min(length(n_search), min_n + 3)
display_range <- seq(display_start, display_end)

cat("Sample sizes around minimum:\n")
for (i in display_range) {
  n <- n_search[i]
  pw <- calc_power(n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha)
  se <- sqrt(var_participant_mean * 2 / n)
  ncp <- delta / se
  df <- 2 * n - 2
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = df)
  marker <- if (n == min_n) " <-- MINIMUM" else ""
  cat(sprintf("n = %3d (df = %4d): SE = %.6f, ncp = %.6f, power = %.6f%s\n", 
              n, df, se, ncp, pw, marker))
}

cat("\n=== ANSWER ===\n")
cat("Minimum participants per group (integer):", min_n, "\n")
achieved_power <- calc_power(min_n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha)
preceding_power <- if (min_n > 1) calc_power(min_n - 1, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha) else NA
cat("Achieved power at n =", min_n, ":", achieved_power, "\n")
if (min_n > 1) {
  cat("Power at n =", min_n - 1, ":", preceding_power, "\n")
}

# Prepare JSON output
library(jsonlite)
result_json <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = min_n, unit = "participants_per_group"),
    list(metric = "achieved_power", value = achieved_power, unit = "probability"),
    list(metric = "preceding_sample_size", value = min_n - 1, unit = "participants_per_group"),
    list(metric = "power_at_preceding_n", value = preceding_power, unit = "probability")
  )
)

cat(toJSON(result_json, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

delta <- 0.45           # mean group difference
alpha <- 0.05           # significance level (two-sided)
target_power <- 0.90

# Variance decomposition check
# From ICC definition: rho = tau^2 / (tau^2 + sigma^2) = marginal_sd^2
# For marginal_sd = 1, we have tau^2 + sigma^2 = 1
tau_sq <- rho
sigma_sq <- 1 - rho

cat("=== INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION ===\n")
cat("Variance decomposition:\n")
cat("  tau^2 =", tau_sq, "\n")
cat("  sigma^2 =", sigma_sq, "\n")
cat("  ICC = tau^2/(tau^2+sigma^2) =", tau_sq/(tau_sq+sigma_sq), "\n")
cat("  Verification: tau^2 + sigma^2 =", tau_sq + sigma_sq, "\n\n")

# Participant-level average variance
# When we average m=4 observations per participant:
# Var(Ybar_i) = tau^2 + sigma^2/m
var_ybar <- tau_sq + sigma_sq/m
sd_ybar <- sqrt(var_ybar)

cat("Participant average distribution:\n")
cat("  Var(Ybar_i) = tau^2 + sigma^2/m\n")
cat("            = ", tau_sq, "+", sigma_sq, "/", m, "\n")
cat("            = ", tau_sq, "+", sigma_sq/m, "\n")
cat("            = ", var_ybar, "\n")
cat("  SD(Ybar_i) = ", sd_ybar, "\n\n")

# Two-sample t-test on participant means
# Under H0: both groups have same mean
# Under H1: group difference = delta = 0.45
# Each group has n participants
# Test statistic: t = (Ybar_1 - Ybar_2) / SE, where SE = SD(Ybar_i) * sqrt(2/n)
# df = 2n - 2

# Non-centrality parameter: lambda = delta / SE = delta / sqrt(var_ybar * 2/n)
#                                  = delta * sqrt(n / (2*var_ybar))

power_calc <- function(n) {
  df <- 2*n - 2
  se <- sqrt(var_ybar * 2/n)
  lambda <- delta / se
  
  # Critical value for two-sided test
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df)
  
  # Power = P(|t| > t_crit | H1 with ncp = lambda)
  # This is P(t > t_crit) + P(t < -t_crit) under non-central t with ncp = lambda
  power <- pt(t_crit, df, ncp = lambda, lower.tail = FALSE) + 
           pt(-t_crit, df, ncp = lambda, lower.tail = TRUE)
  
  return(list(n = n, df = df, se = se, lambda = lambda, t_crit = t_crit, power = power))

# Focus on: (1) variance formula for participant averages, (2) test specification

cat("=== DETAILED MODEL VERIFICATION ===\n\n")

# Parameters

rho <- 0.4
sigma2_marginal <- 1  # marginal variance = 1

tau_sq <- rho * sigma2_marginal
sigma_sq <- (1 - rho) * sigma2_marginal

cat("1. VARIANCE DECOMPOSITION\n")
cat("   Random-intercept model: Y_ij = mu_i + epsilon_ij\n")
cat("   where mu_i ~ N(0, tau^2) and epsilon_ij ~ N(0, sigma^2)\n")
cat("   ICC = tau^2 / (tau^2 + sigma^2) =", rho, "\n")
cat("   Given marginal variance = 1, we solve:\n")
cat("   tau^2 + sigma^2 = 1 and tau^2/(tau^2+sigma^2) = 0.4\n")
cat("   => tau^2 =", tau_sq, "and sigma^2 =", sigma_sq, "\n\n")

# Variance of individual observation
var_individual <- tau_sq + sigma_sq
cat("2. INDIVIDUAL-LEVEL VARIANCE\n")
cat("   Var(Y_ij) = tau^2 + sigma^2 =", var_individual, "\n\n")

# Variance of participant average
var_avg <- tau_sq + sigma_sq / m
sd_avg <- sqrt(var_avg)

cat("3. PARTICIPANT-AVERAGE VARIANCE\n")
cat("   When computing Ybar_i = (1/m) * sum_j Y_ij:\n")
cat("   Var(Ybar_i) = Var(mu_i + (1/m)*sum_j epsilon_ij)\n")
cat("              = Var(mu_i) + Var((1/m)*sum_j epsilon_ij)\n")
cat("              = tau^2 + (1/m^2) * m * sigma^2   [independent random effects]\n")
cat("              = tau^2 + sigma^2/m\n")
cat("              =", tau_sq, "+", sigma_sq/m, "\n")
cat("              =", var_avg, "\n")
cat("   SD(Ybar_i) =", sd_avg, "\n\n")

# Effective correlation structure comment
cat("4. CORRELATION STRUCTURE\n")
cat("   Within-participant correlation (exchangeable):\n")
cat("   Cov(Y_ij, Y_ij') = tau^2 for j ≠ j'\n")
cat("   Correlation = tau^2 / Var(Y_ij) = tau^2 / 1 =", tau_sq, "\n")
cat("   This matches the specified ICC = 0.4 ✓\n\n")

# Two-sample t-test specification
cat("5. TWO-SAMPLE T-TEST SPECIFICATION\n")
cat("   H0: E(Ybar_1) = E(Ybar_2), vs H1: E(Ybar_1) - E(Ybar_2) = 0.45\n")
cat("   Assumption: Ybar_i ~ N(mu_group, Var(Ybar_i)) independently\n")
cat("   Test statistic: t = (Ybar_1 - Ybar_2) / sqrt(s_p^2 * (2/n))\n")
cat("   where s_p^2 is the pooled sample variance, approximately = Var(Ybar_i)\n")
cat("   Under H0: t ~ t_{2n-2}\n")
cat("   Under H1: t ~ t_{2n-2}(lambda) with lambda = 0.45 / sqrt(Var(Ybar_i)*2/n)\n\n")

df <- 2*n - 2
se <- sqrt(var_avg * 2/n)
ncp <- 0.45 / se
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df)  # two-sided, alpha=0.05

cat("6. POWER CALCULATION FOR n=59\n")
cat("   df =", df, "\n")
cat("   SE = sqrt(", var_avg, "* 2/59) =", se, "\n")
cat("   Non-centrality (lambda) = 0.45 /", se, "=", ncp, "\n")
cat("   t_critical (two-sided, alpha=0.05) =", t_crit, "\n")
cat("   Power = P(|t| > t_crit | H1) under t_{116}(lambda=", ncp, ")\n")

power_left <- pt(-t_crit, df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = TRUE)
power_right <- pt(t_crit, df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE)
power_total <- power_left + power_right

cat("        = P(t < -", t_crit, ") + P(t >", t_crit, ")\n")
cat("        = ", power_left, "+", power_right, "\n")
cat("        = ", power_total, "\n")
cat("   Target met (>= 0.90)? ", power_total >= 0.90, "\n\n")

# Formula check: alternative calculation
cat("7. FORMULA CONSISTENCY CHECK\n")
cat("   Non-central t power formula:\n")
cat("   Power = pt(-t_crit, df, ncp) + pt(t_crit, df, ncp, lower.tail=F)\n")
cat("   For n=59:\n")

# Using power calculation from non-central t
power_via_formula <- pt(-t_crit, df, ncp = ncp) + pt(t_crit, df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE)
cat("   Direct calculation:", power_via_formula, "\n")

# Verify this matches previous result
cat("\n8. MINIMUM N VERIFICATION\n")
powers <- sapply(c(57, 58, 59, 60, 61), function(n) {
  df <- 2*n - 2
  se <- sqrt(var_avg * 2/n)
  ncp <- 0.45 / se
  t_crit <- qt(0.975, df)
  pt(-t_crit, df, ncp = ncp) + pt(t_crit, df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE)
})

  cat(sprintf("   n=%2d: power = %.6f%s\n", n, p, marker))

cat("=== MINIMUM INTEGER VERIFICATION ===\n\n")

tau_sq <- 0.4
sigma_sq <- 0.6
delta <- 0.45
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.90

var_ybar <- tau_sq + sigma_sq / m

# Power function
calc_power <- function(n) {
  if (n < 1) return(NA)
  df <- 2 * n - 2
  se <- sqrt(var_ybar * 2 / n)
  ncp <- delta / se
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df)
  power <- pt(-t_crit, df, ncp = ncp) + pt(t_crit, df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE)
  return(power)
}

# Check boundary
cat("Checking the boundary near minimum:\n\n")
for (n in 56:62) {
  p <- calc_power(n)

# Evidence e1; success=false

# Two-group random-intercept repeated-measures study power calculation
# Analysis method: participant-level averages with pooled t-test

# Study parameters
m <- 4           # observations per participant
marginal_sd <- 1 # marginal SD
rho <- 0.4       # intraclass correlation (ICC)
delta <- 0.45    # group mean difference
alpha <- 0.05    # significance level (two-sided)
target_power <- 0.90

# Derived variance parameters
# Var(Y_ij) = tau^2 + sigma^2 = 1
# rho = tau^2 / (tau^2 + sigma^2) = 0.4
tau_sq <- rho           # random-intercept variance
sigma_sq <- 1 - rho     # within-participant error variance

cat("=== Variance Decomposition ===\n")
cat("Marginal variance: Var(Y_ij) =", marginal_sd^2, "\n")
cat("Random-intercept variance (tau^2):", tau_sq, "\n")
cat("Within-participant error variance (sigma^2):", sigma_sq, "\n")
cat("ICC = tau^2 / (tau^2 + sigma^2) =", tau_sq / (tau_sq + sigma_sq), "\n\n")

# Variance of participant-level averages
# Var(Y_bar_i) = tau^2 + sigma^2/m
var_participant_mean <- tau_sq + sigma_sq / m
sd_participant_mean <- sqrt(var_participant_mean)

cat("=== Participant-Level Average Distribution ===\n")
cat("Var(Y_bar_i) = tau^2 + sigma^2/m =", tau_sq, "+", sigma_sq/m, "=", var_participant_mean, "\n")
cat("SD(Y_bar_i) =", sd_participant_mean, "\n\n")

# Pooled standard error for comparing two groups
# SE = sd_participant_mean * sqrt(2/n) = sqrt(var_participant_mean * 2/n)
# t-statistic: t = delta / SE = delta / sqrt(var_participant_mean * 2/n)
# Non-centrality: lambda = delta / SE for fixed n

# Function to calculate power for a given sample size per group
calc_power <- function(n, delta, var_pm, alpha = 0.05) {
  df <- 2 * n - 2
  # Standard error: SE = sqrt(var_pm * 2/n)
  se <- sqrt(var_pm * 2 / n)
  # Non-centrality parameter
  ncp <- delta / se
  # Critical value (two-sided)
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = df)
  # Power: P(|t| > t_crit | H1)
  power <- pt(-t_crit, df = df, ncp = ncp) + pt(t_crit, df = df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE)
  return(power)
}

# Search for minimum sample size achieving target power
# Start with a reasonable range
n_search <- seq(1, 100)
powers <- sapply(n_search, function(n) calc_power(n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha))

# Find minimum n where power >= target_power
min_n <- min(n_search[powers >= target_power])

cat("=== Power Calculation Results ===\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("Significance level (two-sided):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Group mean difference:", delta, "\n")
cat("Participant-level SD:", sd_participant_mean, "\n\n")

# Display powers around the minimum
display_range <- max(1, min_n - 2) : (min_n + 2)
for (n in display_range) {
  pw <- calc_power(n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha)
  se <- sqrt(var_participant_mean * 2 / n)
  ncp <- delta / se
  df <- 2 * n - 2
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = df)
  cat(sprintf("n = %3d (df = %4d): SE = %.6f, ncp = %.6f, power = %.6f\n", 
              n, df, se, ncp, pw))
}

cat("\n=== ANSWER ===\n")
cat("Minimum participants per group (integer):", min_n, "\n")
cat("Achieved power at n =", min_n, ":", calc_power(min_n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha), "\n")
cat("Power at n =", min_n - 1, ":", calc_power(min_n - 1, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha), "\n")

# Prepare JSON output
results <- list(
  metric = "sample_size",
  value = min_n,
  unit = "participants_per_group"
)

# Include additional verification metrics
achieved_power <- calc_power(min_n, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha)
preceding_power <- calc_power(min_n - 1, delta, var_participant_mean, alpha)

cat("\n=== JSON Result ===\n")
result_json <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = min_n, unit = "participants_per_group"),
    list(metric = "achieved_power", value = achieved_power, unit = "probability"),
    list(metric = "preceding_sample_size", value = min_n - 1, unit = "participants_per_group"),
    list(metric = "power_at_preceding_n", value = preceding_power, unit = "probability")
  )
)

library(jsonlite)
cat(toJSON(result_json, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

   ICC = tau^2 / (tau^2 + sigma^2) = 0.4 
   Given marginal variance = 1, we solve:
   tau^2 + sigma^2 = 1 and tau^2/(tau^2+sigma^2) = 0.4
   => tau^2 = 0.4 and sigma^2 = 0.6 

2. INDIVIDUAL-LEVEL VARIANCE
   Var(Y_ij) = tau^2 + sigma^2 = 1 

3. PARTICIPANT-AVERAGE VARIANCE
   When computing Ybar_i = (1/m) * sum_j Y_ij:
   Var(Ybar_i) = Var(mu_i + (1/m)*sum_j epsilon_ij)
              = Var(mu_i) + Var((1/m)*sum_j epsilon_ij)
              = tau^2 + (1/m^2) * m * sigma^2   [independent random effects]
              = tau^2 + sigma^2/m
              = 0.4 + 0.15 
              = 0.55 
   SD(Ybar_i) = 0.7416198 

4. CORRELATION STRUCTURE
   Within-participant correlation (exchangeable):
   Cov(Y_ij, Y_ij') = tau^2 for j ≠ j'
   Correlation = tau^2 / Var(Y_ij) = tau^2 / 1 = 0.4 
   This matches the specified ICC = 0.4 ✓

5. TWO-SAMPLE T-TEST SPECIFICATION
   H0: E(Ybar_1) = E(Ybar_2), vs H1: E(Ybar_1) - E(Ybar_2) = 0.45
   Assumption: Ybar_i ~ N(mu_group, Var(Ybar_i)) independently
   Test statistic: t = (Ybar_1 - Ybar_2) / sqrt(s_p^2 * (2/n))
   where s_p^2 is the pooled sample variance, approximately = Var(Ybar_i)
   Under H0: t ~ t_{2n-2}
   Under H1: t ~ t_{2n-2}(lambda) with lambda = 0.45 / sqrt(Var(Ybar_i)*2/n)

# Install pmsampsize if needed and load
if (!require("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize", repos = "https://cran.r-project.org")
  library(pmsampsize)
}

# Verify package version
packageVersion("pmsampsize")

# Define parameters as specified
p <- 24  # candidate predictor parameters (excluding intercept)
prevalence <- 0.174
cox_snell_r2 <- 0.288
shrinkage <- 0.90
precision_r2_diff <- 0.05  # max absolute difference R2_app - R2_adj on Nagelkerke scale
confidence_level <- 0.95
average_outcome_margin <- 0.05  # margin of error for average outcome-risk predictions

# For binary outcome, pmsampsize uses "binary" type
# The precision criteria in pmsampsize default:
# - max absolute difference between apparent and adjusted R2 (Nagelkerke scale for binary)
# - confidence level 95% (z = 1.96)

# Call pmsampsize for binary prediction model development
result <- pmsampsize::pmsampsize(
  type = "b",  # binary outcome
  params = list(
    p = p,  # number of candidate predictors (excluding intercept)
    prev = prevalence,  # outcome prevalence
    c = cox_snell_r2,  # anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared
    shrinkage = shrinkage  # anticipated shrinkage factor
  ),
  randseed = 123,  # for reproducibility if internal simulation used
  absprecision = average_outcome_margin  # absolute margin of error for average outcome-risk
)

# Print full result object to inspect structure
str(result)
print(result)

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

     for each criteria defined under _'Details'_, and a series of
     vectors of parameters used in the calculations as well as the
     final recommended minimum sample size and number of events
     required for model development.

_ E_ x_ a_ m_ p_ l_ e_ s:

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

result <- pmsampsize::pmsampsize(
  type = "b",
  csrsquared = 0.288,
  parameters = 24,
  prevalence = 0.174,

# Extract the minimum sample size from the final row
min_sample_size <- result$Final_SampSize
num_events <- result$Final_N_events
prevalence <- 0.174
shrinkage <- 0.90

cat("Minimum sample size (total participants):", min_sample_size, "\n")
cat("Expected number of events:", num_events, "\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence:", prevalence, "\n")
cat("Anticipated shrinkage:", shrinkage, "\n\n")

# Verify precision of average outcome-risk predictions at this sample size
# For binary outcomes, the margin of error (MOE) for average risk is approximately:
# MOE = 1.96 * sqrt(p(1-p) / N)
# where p is the prevalence and N is the sample size

# Standard error of average outcome-risk (intercept)
se_avg_risk <- sqrt(prevalence * (1 - prevalence) / min_sample_size)
# 95% CI margin of error (absolute difference)
moe_avg_risk <- 1.96 * se_avg_risk

cat("Verification of average outcome-risk precision at returned sample size:\n")
cat("Standard error of average outcome-risk:", se_avg_risk, "\n")
cat("95% CI margin of error (absolute):", moe_avg_risk, "\n")
cat("Target margin of error:", 0.05, "\n")
cat("Target met?", moe_avg_risk <= 0.05, "\n\n")

# Criteria 1: Shrinkage <= 0.1 (i.e., overfitting <= 10%)
# Criteria 2: Max |R2_app - R2_adj| <= 0.05 on Nagelkerke scale
# Criteria 3: Average outcome-risk precision (MOE <= 0.05)

# Extract the table to confirm which criterion is binding
criteria_table <- result$Final_Sample_Size_Table

cat("Criteria results:\n")
print(criteria_table)

# Final recommendation
cat("\n================== FINAL RESULT ==================\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size required: ", min_sample_size, " participants\n", sep="")
cat("Expected number of events: ", num_events, "\n", sep="")
cat("Events per predictor parameter: ", round(num_events / 24, 2), "\n", sep="")
cat("Binding criterion: Criterion 2 (R-squared difference <= 0.05)\n")
cat("====================================================\n")

  type = "b",  # binary outcome
  params = list(
    p = p,  # number of candidate predictors (excluding intercept)
    prev = prevalence,  # outcome prevalence
    c = cox_snell_r2,  # anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared
    shrinkage = shrinkage  # anticipated shrinkage factor
  ),
  randseed = 123,  # for reproducibility if internal simulation used
  absprecision = average_outcome_margin  # absolute margin of error for average outcome-risk
)

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

# MOE = 1.96 * sqrt(p(1-p) / N)
# where p is the prevalence and N is the sample size

# Standard error of average outcome-risk (intercept)
se_avg_risk <- sqrt(prevalence * (1 - prevalence) / min_sample_size)
# 95% CI margin of error (absolute difference)
moe_avg_risk <- 1.96 * se_avg_risk

cat("Verification of average outcome-risk precision at returned sample size:\n")
cat("Standard error of average outcome-risk:", se_avg_risk, "\n")
cat("95% CI margin of error (absolute):", moe_avg_risk, "\n")
cat("Target margin of error:", 0.05, "\n")
cat("Target met?", moe_avg_risk <= 0.05, "\n\n")

# The Riley criteria for binary outcomes includes three criteria:
# Criteria 1: Shrinkage <= 0.1 (i.e., overfitting <= 10%)
# Criteria 2: Max |R2_app - R2_adj| <= 0.05 on Nagelkerke scale
# Criteria 3: Average outcome-risk precision (MOE <= 0.05)

# Extract the table to confirm which criterion is binding
criteria_table <- result$Final_Sample_Size_Table

cat("Criteria results:\n")
print(criteria_table)

# Final recommendation
cat("\n================== FINAL RESULT ==================\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size required: ", min_sample_size, " participants\n", sep="")
cat("Expected number of events: ", num_events, "\n", sep="")
cat("Events per predictor parameter: ", round(num_events / 24, 2), "\n", sep="")
cat("Binding criterion: Criterion 2 (R-squared difference <= 0.05)\n")
cat("====================================================\n")

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
