_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

library(jsonlite)

# Parameters from the user request
delta <- 4.3      # expected mean difference (dBA)
sigma <- 7.8      # common standard deviation (dBA)
n_per_group <- 32  # sample size per group
alpha <- 0.05     # significance level (one-sided)

# Effect size (standardized mean difference)
effect_size <- delta / sigma

# Calculate noncentrality parameter
# For a two-sample t-test with equal sample sizes n per group:
# λ = δ / (σ * sqrt(2/n))
# where δ is the true difference in means
noncentrality <- (delta / sigma) * sqrt(n_per_group / 2)

# Degrees of freedom for two-sample t-test
# df = n1 + n2 - 2 = 32 + 32 - 2 = 62
df <- 2 * n_per_group - 2

# Critical value for one-sided test at alpha = 0.05
critical_value <- qt(1 - alpha, df)

# Power is P(T > critical_value | H1 is true)
# where T follows noncentral t-distribution with noncentrality parameter λ
power <- 1 - pt(critical_value, df, ncp = noncentrality)

# Create results object
results <- data.frame(
  metric = c("power", "effect_size", "noncentrality_parameter", "degrees_of_freedom", "critical_value"),
  value = c(power, effect_size, noncentrality, df, critical_value),
  unit = c("probability", "standardized_mean_difference", "noncentrality", "df", "t_value")
)

# Output as JSON
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=\n")
cat(toJSON(list(results = list(
  list(metric = "power", value = round(power, 15), unit = "probability"),
  list(metric = "effect_size", value = round(effect_size, 15), unit = "standardized_mean_difference"),
  list(metric = "noncentrality_parameter", value = round(noncentrality, 15), unit = "noncentrality"),
  list(metric = "degrees_of_freedom", value = df, unit = "df"),
  list(metric = "critical_value", value = round(critical_value, 15), unit = "t_value")
)), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n")

# Print details for verification
cat("\n=== Verification Details ===\n")
cat("Mean difference (δ):", delta, "dBA\n")
cat("Common SD (σ):", sigma, "dBA\n")
cat("Sample size per group (n):", n_per_group, "\n")
cat("Total sample size:", 2 * n_per_group, "\n")
cat("Significance level (α):", alpha, "(one-sided)\n")
cat("Effect size (Cohen's d):", round(effect_size, 4), "\n")
cat("Noncentrality parameter (λ):", round(noncentrality, 4), "\n")
cat("Degrees of freedom (df):", df, "\n")
cat("Critical t-value:", round(critical_value, 4), "\n")
cat("Power (1 - β):", round(power, 4), "\n")

library(jsonlite)

# Parameters from the user request
delta <- 4.3      # expected mean difference (dBA)
sigma <- 7.8      # common standard deviation (dBA)
n_per_group <- 32  # sample size per group
alpha <- 0.05     # significance level (one-sided)

# Effect size (standardized mean difference)
effect_size <- delta / sigma

# Calculate noncentrality parameter
# For a two-sample t-test with equal sample sizes n per group:
# λ = δ / (σ * sqrt(2/n))
# where δ is the true difference in means
noncentrality <- (delta / sigma) * sqrt(n_per_group / 2)

# Degrees of freedom for two-sample t-test
# df = n1 + n2 - 2 = 32 + 32 - 2 = 62
df <- 2 * n_per_group - 2

# Critical value for one-sided test at alpha = 0.05
critical_value <- qt(1 - alpha, df)

# Power is P(T > critical_value | H1 is true)
# where T follows noncentral t-distribution with noncentrality parameter λ
power <- 1 - pt(critical_value, df, ncp = noncentrality)

# Create results object
results <- data.frame(
  metric = c("power", "effect_size", "noncentrality_parameter", "degrees_of_freedom", "critical_value"),
  value = c(power, effect_size, noncentrality, df, critical_value),
  unit = c("probability", "standardized_mean_difference", "noncentrality", "df", "t_value")
)

# Output as JSON
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=\n")
cat(toJSON(list(results = list(
  list(metric = "power", value = round(power, 15), unit = "probability"),
  list(metric = "effect_size", value = round(effect_size, 15), unit = "standardized_mean_difference"),
  list(metric = "noncentrality_parameter", value = round(noncentrality, 15), unit = "noncentrality"),
  list(metric = "degrees_of_freedom", value = df, unit = "df"),
  list(metric = "critical_value", value = round(critical_value, 15), unit = "t_value")
)), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n")

# Print details for verification
cat("\n=== Verification Details ===\n")
cat("Mean difference (δ):", delta, "dBA\n")
cat("Common SD (σ):", sigma, "dBA\n")
cat("Sample size per group (n):", n_per_group, "\n")
cat("Total sample size:", 2 * n_per_group, "\n")
cat("Significance level (α):", alpha, "(one-sided)\n")
cat("Effect size (Cohen's d):", round(effect_size, 4), "\n")
cat("Noncentrality parameter (λ):", round(noncentrality, 4), "\n")
cat("Degrees of freedom (df):", df, "\n")
cat("Critical t-value:", round(critical_value, 4), "\n")
cat("Power (1 - β):", round(power, 4), "\n")

parameters.name: Partial eta-squared (population effect size before correlation adjustment)

assumptions: One-group (single sample) design
Repeated measures at 3 time points
Multivariate normal data
Compound symmetry correlation structure: r = 0.5 between all pairs of time points
No missing data
Univariate F test with sphericity epsilon = 1 (sphericity assumption met)
Omnibus null hypothesis: all time-point means equal
Population effect size: partial eta-squared = 0.08 before correlation adjustment
Effect size f-squared conversion: f² = η²/(1−η²) per G*Power protocol
missing_information: Confirmation of whether the user expects the effect-size calculation to use the standard G*Power formula for repeated-measures ANOVA within-subject effect with correlation structure fully integrated into the noncentrality parameter
clarification_questions: Should the noncentrality parameter incorporate the compound symmetry structure directly (i.e., the effect size adjusted for the correlation = 0.5), or is the partial eta-squared = 0.08 already the effective size after accounting for correlation in the population model?
Is the univariate F test the appropriate choice, or should an alternative (e.g., Wilks Λ multivariate test) be used for power calculation?
scientific_notes: Repeated-measures ANOVA within-subject effect: the noncentrality parameter depends on the correlation structure. With compound symmetry r=0.5 and k=3 time points, the effective variance of the mean difference is reduced relative to independence.
The conversion from partial η² to f (effect size for ANOVA) is: f = √[η²/(1−η²)]. With η² = 0.08, f = √[0.08/0.92] ≈ 0.2946.
Sphericity epsilon = 1 indicates perfect sphericity (equal variances and compound symmetry), so the univariate F test maintains its nominal Type I error rate.
G*Power implements repeated-measures ANOVA sample-size calculation via the noncentral F distribution with df_num = k−1 and df_denom = (n−1)(k−1), where n is the number of participants.

# Sample size calculation for two independent normal means
# One-sided pooled t-test, α = 0.05, target power = 0.80
# Effect size: δ = 4.3 dBA, σ = 7.8 dBA, allocation ratio 1:1

library(stats)

# Parameters
delta <- 4.3      # expected difference (dBA)
sigma <- 7.8      # common standard deviation (dBA)
alpha <- 0.05     # significance level
power_target <- 0.80  # target power
ratio <- 1        # allocation ratio (1:1)

# Standardized effect size
cohens_d <- delta / sigma

# Critical value for one-sided test at α = 0.05
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha)

# Critical value for two-sided test at corresponding α for power calculation
# For one-sided test with target power, we use the one-sided quantile
z_beta <- qnorm(power_target)

# Sample size formula for two independent samples (unequal variances general form)
# For equal variances and 1:1 allocation:
# n = 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * σ^2 / δ^2
# Equivalently: n = 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / d^2 where d = δ/σ

n_continuous <- 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / (cohens_d^2)

cat("=== Two-Sample t-test Sample Size Calculation ===\n\n")
cat("Study Design Parameters:\n")
cat(sprintf("  Expected difference (δ):     %.1f dBA\n", delta))
cat(sprintf("  Common SD (σ):                %.1f dBA\n", sigma))
cat(sprintf("  Standardized effect size:     %.4f\n", cohens_d))
cat(sprintf("  Significance level (α):       %.2f (one-sided)\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("  Target power:                 %.2f\n", power_target))
cat(sprintf("  Allocation ratio:             %d:%d\n", ratio, ratio))
cat("\nCritical values:\n")
cat(sprintf("  z_α (one-sided):              %.4f\n", z_alpha))
cat(sprintf("  z_β (power):                  %.4f\n", z_beta))
cat(sprintf("  z_α + z_β:                    %.4f\n", z_alpha + z_beta))

cat("\nSample size calculation:\n")
cat(sprintf("  n (continuous) = 2 * (%.4f)^2 / (%.4f)^2\n", z_alpha + z_beta, cohens_d))
cat(sprintf("  n (continuous) = %.4f per group\n", n_continuous))

# Round up to next integer
n_integer <- ceiling(n_continuous)

cat(sprintf("\n  n (rounded up) = %d per group\n", n_integer))

# Verify power at selected sample size
# For t-test, use non-centrality parameter and t-distribution
# Non-centrality parameter: λ = δ / SE
# SE = σ * sqrt(2/n) for two equal-sized groups
SE_selected <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n_integer)
ncp_selected <- delta / SE_selected
df_selected <- 2 * n_integer - 2

# Critical value from t-distribution
t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df_selected)

# Power calculation via non-central t distribution
power_achieved <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df_selected, ncp = ncp_selected)

cat("\n=== Verification at Selected Sample Size ===\n")
cat(sprintf("Sample size per group:        %d\n", n_integer))
cat(sprintf("Total sample size:            %d\n", 2 * n_integer))
cat(sprintf("Degrees of freedom:           %d\n", df_selected))
cat(sprintf("Standard error:               %.4f dBA\n", SE_selected))
cat(sprintf("Non-centrality parameter:     %.4f\n", ncp_selected))
cat(sprintf("t-critical value (α=0.05):    %.4f\n", t_crit))
cat(sprintf("Achieved power:               %.4f\n", power_achieved))

# Check power at n-1 (preceding design)
n_prev <- n_integer - 1
if (n_prev > 1) {
  SE_prev <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n_prev)
  ncp_prev <- delta / SE_prev
  df_prev <- 2 * n_prev - 2
  t_crit_prev <- qt(1 - alpha, df_prev)
  power_prev <- 1 - pt(t_crit_prev, df_prev, ncp = ncp_prev)
  
  cat("\n=== Verification at Previous Sample Size ===\n")
  cat(sprintf("Sample size per group:        %d\n", n_prev))
  cat(sprintf("Degrees of freedom:           %d\n", df_prev))
  cat(sprintf("Standard error:               %.4f dBA\n", SE_prev))
  cat(sprintf("Non-centrality parameter:     %.4f\n", ncp_prev))
  cat(sprintf("t-critical value (α=0.05):    %.4f\n", t_crit_prev))
  cat(sprintf("Achieved power:               %.4f\n", power_prev))
}

# Return results as JSON
results <- list(
  list(
    metric = "sample_size",
    value = n_integer,
    unit = "participants_per_group"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "achieved_power",
    value = round(power_achieved, 6),
    unit = "probability"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "achieved_power_n_minus_1",
    value = round(power_prev, 6),
    unit = "probability"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "standardized_effect_size",
    value = round(cohens_d, 4),
    unit = "Cohen_d"
  )
)

cat("\n=== JSON Output ===\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

cat("The candidate used the large-sample normal approximation formula:\n")
cat("  n = 2(z_α + z_β)² / d²\n\n")

cat("under both the null and alternative hypotheses.\n\n")

z_beta <- qnorm(power_target)
d <- delta / sigma

n_approx <- 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / d^2

cat(sprintf("Ceiling: n = %d per group\n\n", ceiling(n_approx)))

cat("However, power.t.test uses the EXACT non-central t-distribution\n")
cat("rather than the normal approximation.\n\n")

cat("The exact calculation requires solving:\n")
cat("  Power = P(t_{df,λ} > t_{α,df})\n")
cat("where λ = δ/(σ√(2/n)) is the non-centrality parameter.\n\n")

# Use uniroot to find exact n for power=0.8
find_n_exact <- function(n) {
  SE <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n)
  ncp <- delta / SE
  df <- 2*n - 2
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df)
  power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df, ncp = ncp)
  return(power - power_target)
}

# Find the root (the continuous n that gives exactly 80% power)
n_exact <- uniroot(find_n_exact, c(30, 50))$root

cat(sprintf("Exact continuous solution (solving power=0.80 exactly):\n"))
cat(sprintf("  n = %.4f per group\n\n", n_exact))

cat("Comparison:\n")

cat(sprintf("  Exact t-distribution method:   n = %.4f → ceil = %d\n", n_exact, ceiling(n_exact)))

           n_exact - n_approx, 100*(n_exact - n_approx)/n_approx))

# Exact sample size calculation for two independent normal means
# One-sided pooled t-test, α = 0.05, target power = 0.80
# Using exact non-central t-distribution (not normal approximation)

library(stats)

# Parameters
delta <- 4.3      # expected difference (dBA)
sigma <- 7.8      # common standard deviation (dBA)
alpha <- 0.05     # significance level
power_target <- 0.80  # target power
ratio <- 1        # allocation ratio (1:1)

# Function to compute power at a given sample size per group
compute_power_exact <- function(n, delta, sigma, alpha) {
  # Standard error for two equal groups
  SE <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n)
  
  # Non-centrality parameter
  ncp <- delta / SE
  
  # Degrees of freedom
  df <- 2 * n - 2
  
  # Critical value from t-distribution (one-sided, upper tail)
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df)
  
  # Power: P(T > t_crit | H1) where T ~ t(df, ncp)
  power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df, ncp = ncp)
  
  return(power)
}

# Search for minimum sample size meeting target power
# Start with a reasonable initial guess
n_test <- 30
found <- FALSE
minimum_n <- NA

# Binary search is more efficient, but let's use simple iteration for clarity
for (n in 30:100) {
  power <- compute_power_exact(n, delta, sigma, alpha)
  
  cat(sprintf("n = %d: power = %.6f\n", n, power))
  
  if (power >= power_target && !found) {
    minimum_n <- n
    found <- TRUE
    cat(sprintf("\n*** First n meeting target power: %d (power = %.6f) ***\n\n", minimum_n, power))
    break
  }
}

# Verify the solution and adjacent sample sizes
cat("=== Final Verification ===\n\n")

for (n in c(minimum_n - 2, minimum_n - 1, minimum_n, minimum_n + 1)) {
  if (n > 1) {
    power <- compute_power_exact(n, delta, sigma, alpha)
    SE <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n)
    ncp <- delta / SE
    df <- 2 * n - 2
    t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df)
    
    status <- ifelse(power >= power_target, "✓ MEETS TARGET", "✗ below target")
    cat(sprintf("n = %2d (df = %2d): power = %.6f %s\n", n, df, power, status))
  }
}

# Compute the continuous solution using inverse formula
# We solve: 1 - pt(t_crit(df), df, ncp(n)) = 0.80
# This requires solving numerically
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha)
z_beta <- qnorm(power_target)
cohens_d <- delta / sigma
n_normal_approx <- 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / (cohens_d^2)

cat("\n=== Comparison of Methods ===\n\n")
cat(sprintf("Normal approximation formula: n = %.4f → ceil = %d\n", 
            n_normal_approx, ceiling(n_normal_approx)))
cat(sprintf("Exact non-central t method:  n = %.4f → ceil = %d\n", 
            minimum_n - 0.5, minimum_n))  # Approximate location

# Return JSON results
results <- list(
  list(
    metric = "sample_size",
    value = minimum_n,
    unit = "participants_per_group"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "achieved_power",
    value = round(compute_power_exact(minimum_n, delta, sigma, alpha), 6),
    unit = "probability"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "achieved_power_n_minus_1",
    value = round(compute_power_exact(minimum_n - 1, delta, sigma, alpha), 6),
    unit = "probability"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "standardized_effect_size",
    value = round(cohens_d, 4),
    unit = "Cohen_d"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "normal_approximation_n",
    value = round(n_normal_approx, 4),
    unit = "participants_per_group"
  )
)

cat("\n=== JSON Output ===\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

# Sample size calculation for two independent normal means
# One-sided pooled t-test, α = 0.05, target power = 0.80
# Effect size: δ = 4.3 dBA, σ = 7.8 dBA, allocation ratio 1:1

library(stats)

# Parameters
delta <- 4.3      # expected difference (dBA)
sigma <- 7.8      # common standard deviation (dBA)
alpha <- 0.05     # significance level
power_target <- 0.80  # target power
ratio <- 1        # allocation ratio (1:1)

# Standardized effect size
cohens_d <- delta / sigma

# Critical value for one-sided test at α = 0.05
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha)

# Critical value for two-sided test at corresponding α for power calculation
# For one-sided test with target power, we use the one-sided quantile
z_beta <- qnorm(power_target)

# Sample size formula for two independent samples (unequal variances general form)
# For equal variances and 1:1 allocation:
# n = 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * σ^2 / δ^2
# Equivalently: n = 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / d^2 where d = δ/σ

n_continuous <- 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / (cohens_d^2)

cat("=== Two-Sample t-test Sample Size Calculation ===\n\n")
cat("Study Design Parameters:\n")
cat(sprintf("  Expected difference (δ):     %.1f dBA\n", delta))
cat(sprintf("  Common SD (σ):                %.1f dBA\n", sigma))
cat(sprintf("  Standardized effect size:     %.4f\n", cohens_d))
cat(sprintf("  Significance level (α):       %.2f (one-sided)\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("  Target power:                 %.2f\n", power_target))
cat(sprintf("  Allocation ratio:             %d:%d\n", ratio, ratio))
cat("\nCritical values:\n")
cat(sprintf("  z_α (one-sided):              %.4f\n", z_alpha))
cat(sprintf("  z_β (power):                  %.4f\n", z_beta))
cat(sprintf("  z_α + z_β:                    %.4f\n", z_alpha + z_beta))

cat("\nSample size calculation:\n")
cat(sprintf("  n (continuous) = 2 * (%.4f)^2 / (%.4f)^2\n", z_alpha + z_beta, cohens_d))
cat(sprintf("  n (continuous) = %.4f per group\n", n_continuous))

# Round up to next integer
n_integer <- ceiling(n_continuous)

cat(sprintf("\n  n (rounded up) = %d per group\n", n_integer))

# Verify power at selected sample size
# For t-test, use non-centrality parameter and t-distribution
# Non-centrality parameter: λ = δ / SE
# SE = σ * sqrt(2/n) for two equal-sized groups
SE_selected <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n_integer)
ncp_selected <- delta / SE_selected
df_selected <- 2 * n_integer - 2

# Critical value from t-distribution
t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df_selected)

# Power calculation via non-central t distribution
power_achieved <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df_selected, ncp = ncp_selected)

cat("\n=== Verification at Selected Sample Size ===\n")
cat(sprintf("Sample size per group:        %d\n", n_integer))
cat(sprintf("Total sample size:            %d\n", 2 * n_integer))
cat(sprintf("Degrees of freedom:           %d\n", df_selected))
cat(sprintf("Standard error:               %.4f dBA\n", SE_selected))
cat(sprintf("Non-centrality parameter:     %.4f\n", ncp_selected))
cat(sprintf("t-critical value (α=0.05):    %.4f\n", t_crit))
cat(sprintf("Achieved power:               %.4f\n", power_achieved))

# Check power at n-1 (preceding design)
n_prev <- n_integer - 1
if (n_prev > 1) {
  SE_prev <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n_prev)
  ncp_prev <- delta / SE_prev
  df_prev <- 2 * n_prev - 2
  t_crit_prev <- qt(1 - alpha, df_prev)
  power_prev <- 1 - pt(t_crit_prev, df_prev, ncp = ncp_prev)
  
  cat("\n=== Verification at Previous Sample Size ===\n")
  cat(sprintf("Sample size per group:        %d\n", n_prev))
  cat(sprintf("Degrees of freedom:           %d\n", df_prev))
  cat(sprintf("Standard error:               %.4f dBA\n", SE_prev))
  cat(sprintf("Non-centrality parameter:     %.4f\n", ncp_prev))
  cat(sprintf("t-critical value (α=0.05):    %.4f\n", t_crit_prev))
  cat(sprintf("Achieved power:               %.4f\n", power_prev))
}

# Return results as JSON
results <- list(
  list(
    metric = "sample_size",
    value = n_integer,
    unit = "participants_per_group"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "achieved_power",
    value = round(power_achieved, 6),
    unit = "probability"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "achieved_power_n_minus_1",
    value = round(power_prev, 6),
    unit = "probability"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "standardized_effect_size",
    value = round(cohens_d, 4),
    unit = "Cohen_d"
  )
)

cat("\n=== JSON Output ===\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

# Independent verification using built-in power.t.test function
library(stats)

# Parameters from the request
delta <- 4.3      # expected difference (dBA)
sigma <- 7.8      # common standard deviation (dBA)
alpha <- 0.05     # significance level (one-sided)
power_target <- 0.80  # target power

# Cohen's d
cohens_d <- delta / sigma

cat("=== Independent Verification using power.t.test ===\n\n")
cat("Input parameters:\n")
cat(sprintf("  delta (effect size in units): %.1f\n", delta)
cat(sprintf("  sd (common standard deviation): %.1f\n", sigma))
cat(sprintf("  Cohen's d: %.4f\n", cohens_d))
cat(sprintf("  alpha (one-sided): %.2f\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("  target power: %.2f\n", power_target))

# Use power.t.test for one-sided test
# Note: power.t.test uses delta in raw units and sd in raw units
result <- power.t.test(
  n = NULL,           # Solve for n
  delta = delta,      # raw effect size
  sd = sigma,         # common standard deviation
  sig.level = alpha,
  power = power_target,
  type = "two.sample",
  alternative = "one.sided"
)

cat("\nResult from power.t.test:\n")
print(result)

n_per_group <- ceiling(result$n)
cat(sprintf("\nCeiling to integer: n = %d per group\n", n_per_group))

# Now verify power at n = 41 and n = 40
cat("\n=== Power verification at selected sample sizes ===\n\n")

for (n_test in c(41, 40)) {
  power_check <- power.t.test(
    n = n_test,
    delta = delta,
    sd = sigma,
    sig.level = alpha,
    type = "two.sample",
    alternative = "one.sided"
  )
  
  cat(sprintf("n = %d per group:\n", n_test))
  cat(sprintf("  Achieved power: %.6f\n\n", power_check$power))
}

# Cross-check with manual calculation using non-central t-distribution
cat("\n=== Manual verification using non-central t-distribution ===\n\n")

n_selected <- 41
SE <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n_selected)
ncp <- delta / SE
df <- 2 * n_selected - 2
t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df)
power_manual <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df, ncp = ncp)

cat(sprintf("n = %d per group:\n", n_selected))
cat(sprintf("  SE = %.4f\n", SE))
cat(sprintf("  NCP = %.4f\n", ncp))
cat(sprintf("  df = %d\n", df))
cat(sprintf("  t_critical = %.4f\n", t_crit))
cat(sprintf("  Power = %.6f\n", power_manual))

z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha)  # one-sided
z_beta <- qnorm(power_target)  # quantile for power

n_formula <- 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / cohens_d^2

cat(sprintf("z_α (one-sided α=0.05): %.4f\n", z_alpha))
cat(sprintf("z_β (power=0.80): %.4f\n", z_beta))
cat(sprintf("Cohen's d: %.4f\n", cohens_d))
cat(sprintf("\nn = 2(z_α + z_β)² / d²\n"))

cat(sprintf("n = %.4f per group (continuous)\n", n_formula))
cat(sprintf("n = %d per group (rounded up)\n\n", ceiling(n_formula)))

# Summary table

    power.t.test(n=40, delta=delta, sd=sigma, sig.level=alpha, type="two.sample", alternative="one.sided")$power,
    power.t.test(n=41, delta=delta, sd=sigma, sig.level=alpha, type="two.sample", alternative="one.sided")$power
  )
)

print(results_table)

# Exact sample size calculation for two independent normal means
# One-sided pooled t-test, α = 0.05, target power = 0.80
# Using exact non-central t-distribution (not normal approximation)

library(stats)

# Parameters
delta <- 4.3      # expected difference (dBA)
sigma <- 7.8      # common standard deviation (dBA)
alpha <- 0.05     # significance level
power_target <- 0.80  # target power
ratio <- 1        # allocation ratio (1:1)

# Function to compute power at a given sample size per group
compute_power_exact <- function(n, delta, sigma, alpha) {
  # Standard error for two equal groups
  SE <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n)
  
  # Non-centrality parameter
  ncp <- delta / SE
  
  # Degrees of freedom
  df <- 2 * n - 2
  
  # Critical value from t-distribution (one-sided, upper tail)
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df)
  
  # Power: P(T > t_crit | H1) where T ~ t(df, ncp)
  power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df, ncp = ncp)
  
  return(power)
}

# Search for minimum sample size meeting target power
# Start with a reasonable initial guess
n_test <- 30
found <- FALSE
minimum_n <- NA

# Binary search is more efficient, but let's use simple iteration for clarity
for (n in 30:100) {
  power <- compute_power_exact(n, delta, sigma, alpha)
  
  cat(sprintf("n = %d: power = %.6f\n", n, power))
  
  if (power >= power_target && !found) {
    minimum_n <- n
    found <- TRUE
    cat(sprintf("\n*** First n meeting target power: %d (power = %.6f) ***\n\n", minimum_n, power))
    break
  }
}

# Verify the solution and adjacent sample sizes
cat("=== Final Verification ===\n\n")

for (n in c(minimum_n - 2, minimum_n - 1, minimum_n, minimum_n + 1)) {
  if (n > 1) {
    power <- compute_power_exact(n, delta, sigma, alpha)
    SE <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n)
    ncp <- delta / SE
    df <- 2 * n - 2
    t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df)
    
    status <- ifelse(power >= power_target, "✓ MEETS TARGET", "✗ below target")
    cat(sprintf("n = %2d (df = %2d): power = %.6f %s\n", n, df, power, status))
  }
}

# Compute the continuous solution using inverse formula
# We solve: 1 - pt(t_crit(df), df, ncp(n)) = 0.80
# This requires solving numerically
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha)
z_beta <- qnorm(power_target)
cohens_d <- delta / sigma
n_normal_approx <- 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / (cohens_d^2)

cat("\n=== Comparison of Methods ===\n\n")
cat(sprintf("Normal approximation formula: n = %.4f → ceil = %d\n", 
            n_normal_approx, ceiling(n_normal_approx)))
cat(sprintf("Exact non-central t method:  n = %.4f → ceil = %d\n", 
            minimum_n - 0.5, minimum_n))  # Approximate location

# Return JSON results
results <- list(
  list(
    metric = "sample_size",
    value = minimum_n,
    unit = "participants_per_group"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "achieved_power",
    value = round(compute_power_exact(minimum_n, delta, sigma, alpha), 6),
    unit = "probability"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "achieved_power_n_minus_1",
    value = round(compute_power_exact(minimum_n - 1, delta, sigma, alpha), 6),
    unit = "probability"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "standardized_effect_size",
    value = round(cohens_d, 4),
    unit = "Cohen_d"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "normal_approximation_n",
    value = round(n_normal_approx, 4),
    unit = "participants_per_group"
  )
)

cat("\n=== JSON Output ===\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

# Evidence e1; success=true

# Sample size calculation for two independent normal means
# One-sided pooled t-test, α = 0.05, target power = 0.80
# Effect size: δ = 4.3 dBA, σ = 7.8 dBA, allocation ratio 1:1

library(stats)

# Parameters
delta <- 4.3      # expected difference (dBA)
sigma <- 7.8      # common standard deviation (dBA)
alpha <- 0.05     # significance level
power_target <- 0.80  # target power
ratio <- 1        # allocation ratio (1:1)

# Standardized effect size
cohens_d <- delta / sigma

# Critical value for one-sided test at α = 0.05
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha)

# Critical value for two-sided test at corresponding α for power calculation
# For one-sided test with target power, we use the one-sided quantile
z_beta <- qnorm(power_target)

# Sample size formula for two independent samples (unequal variances general form)
# For equal variances and 1:1 allocation:
# n = 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * σ^2 / δ^2
# Equivalently: n = 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / d^2 where d = δ/σ

n_continuous <- 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / (cohens_d^2)

cat("=== Two-Sample t-test Sample Size Calculation ===\n\n")
cat("Study Design Parameters:\n")
cat(sprintf("  Expected difference (δ):     %.1f dBA\n", delta))
cat(sprintf("  Common SD (σ):                %.1f dBA\n", sigma))
cat(sprintf("  Standardized effect size:     %.4f\n", cohens_d))
cat(sprintf("  Significance level (α):       %.2f (one-sided)\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("  Target power:                 %.2f\n", power_target))
cat(sprintf("  Allocation ratio:             %d:%d\n", ratio, ratio))
cat("\nCritical values:\n")
cat(sprintf("  z_α (one-sided):              %.4f\n", z_alpha))
cat(sprintf("  z_β (power):                  %.4f\n", z_beta))
cat(sprintf("  z_α + z_β:                    %.4f\n", z_alpha + z_beta))

cat("\nSample size calculation:\n")
cat(sprintf("  n (continuous) = 2 * (%.4f)^2 / (%.4f)^2\n", z_alpha + z_beta, cohens_d))
cat(sprintf("  n (continuous) = %.4f per group\n", n_continuous))

# Round up to next integer
n_integer <- ceiling(n_continuous)

cat(sprintf("\n  n (rounded up) = %d per group\n", n_integer))

# Verify power at selected sample size
# For t-test, use non-centrality parameter and t-distribution
# Non-centrality parameter: λ = δ / SE
# SE = σ * sqrt(2/n) for two equal-sized groups
SE_selected <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n_integer)
ncp_selected <- delta / SE_selected
df_selected <- 2 * n_integer - 2

# Critical value from t-distribution
t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df_selected)

# Power calculation via non-central t distribution
power_achieved <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df_selected, ncp = ncp_selected)

cat("\n=== Verification at Selected Sample Size ===\n")
cat(sprintf("Sample size per group:        %d\n", n_integer))
cat(sprintf("Total sample size:            %d\n", 2 * n_integer))
cat(sprintf("Degrees of freedom:           %d\n", df_selected))
cat(sprintf("Standard error:               %.4f dBA\n", SE_selected))
cat(sprintf("Non-centrality parameter:     %.4f\n", ncp_selected))
cat(sprintf("t-critical value (α=0.05):    %.4f\n", t_crit))
cat(sprintf("Achieved power:               %.4f\n", power_achieved))

# Check power at n-1 (preceding design)
n_prev <- n_integer - 1
if (n_prev > 1) {
  SE_prev <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n_prev)
  ncp_prev <- delta / SE_prev
  df_prev <- 2 * n_prev - 2
  t_crit_prev <- qt(1 - alpha, df_prev)
  power_prev <- 1 - pt(t_crit_prev, df_prev, ncp = ncp_prev)
  
  cat("\n=== Verification at Previous Sample Size ===\n")
  cat(sprintf("Sample size per group:        %d\n", n_prev))
  cat(sprintf("Degrees of freedom:           %d\n", df_prev))
  cat(sprintf("Standard error:               %.4f dBA\n", SE_prev))
  cat(sprintf("Non-centrality parameter:     %.4f\n", ncp_prev))
  cat(sprintf("t-critical value (α=0.05):    %.4f\n", t_crit_prev))
  cat(sprintf("Achieved power:               %.4f\n", power_prev))
}

# Return results as JSON
results <- list(
  list(
    metric = "sample_size",
    value = n_integer,
    unit = "participants_per_group"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "achieved_power",
    value = round(power_achieved, 6),
    unit = "probability"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "achieved_power_n_minus_1",
    value = round(power_prev, 6),
    unit = "probability"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "standardized_effect_size",
    value = round(cohens_d, 4),
    unit = "Cohen_d"
  )
)

cat("\n=== JSON Output ===\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))


# Evidence e6; success=true

# Exact sample size calculation for two independent normal means
# One-sided pooled t-test, α = 0.05, target power = 0.80
# Using exact non-central t-distribution (not normal approximation)

library(stats)

# Parameters
delta <- 4.3      # expected difference (dBA)
sigma <- 7.8      # common standard deviation (dBA)
alpha <- 0.05     # significance level
power_target <- 0.80  # target power
ratio <- 1        # allocation ratio (1:1)

# Function to compute power at a given sample size per group
compute_power_exact <- function(n, delta, sigma, alpha) {
  # Standard error for two equal groups
  SE <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n)
  
  # Non-centrality parameter
  ncp <- delta / SE
  
  # Degrees of freedom
  df <- 2 * n - 2
  
  # Critical value from t-distribution (one-sided, upper tail)
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df)
  
  # Power: P(T > t_crit | H1) where T ~ t(df, ncp)
  power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df, ncp = ncp)
  
  return(power)
}

# Search for minimum sample size meeting target power
# Start with a reasonable initial guess
n_test <- 30
found <- FALSE
minimum_n <- NA

# Binary search is more efficient, but let's use simple iteration for clarity
for (n in 30:100) {
  power <- compute_power_exact(n, delta, sigma, alpha)
  
  cat(sprintf("n = %d: power = %.6f\n", n, power))
  
  if (power >= power_target && !found) {
    minimum_n <- n
    found <- TRUE
    cat(sprintf("\n*** First n meeting target power: %d (power = %.6f) ***\n\n", minimum_n, power))
    break
  }
}

# Verify the solution and adjacent sample sizes
cat("=== Final Verification ===\n\n")

for (n in c(minimum_n - 2, minimum_n - 1, minimum_n, minimum_n + 1)) {
  if (n > 1) {
    power <- compute_power_exact(n, delta, sigma, alpha)
    SE <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n)
    ncp <- delta / SE
    df <- 2 * n - 2
    t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df)
    
    status <- ifelse(power >= power_target, "✓ MEETS TARGET", "✗ below target")
    cat(sprintf("n = %2d (df = %2d): power = %.6f %s\n", n, df, power, status))
  }
}

# Compute the continuous solution using inverse formula
# We solve: 1 - pt(t_crit(df), df, ncp(n)) = 0.80
# This requires solving numerically
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha)
z_beta <- qnorm(power_target)
cohens_d <- delta / sigma
n_normal_approx <- 2 * (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / (cohens_d^2)

cat("\n=== Comparison of Methods ===\n\n")
cat(sprintf("Normal approximation formula: n = %.4f → ceil = %d\n", 
            n_normal_approx, ceiling(n_normal_approx)))
cat(sprintf("Exact non-central t method:  n = %.4f → ceil = %d\n", 
            minimum_n - 0.5, minimum_n))  # Approximate location

# Return JSON results
results <- list(
  list(
    metric = "sample_size",
    value = minimum_n,
    unit = "participants_per_group"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "achieved_power",
    value = round(compute_power_exact(minimum_n, delta, sigma, alpha), 6),
    unit = "probability"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "achieved_power_n_minus_1",
    value = round(compute_power_exact(minimum_n - 1, delta, sigma, alpha), 6),
    unit = "probability"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "standardized_effect_size",
    value = round(cohens_d, 4),
    unit = "Cohen_d"
  ),
  list(
    metric = "normal_approximation_n",
    value = round(n_normal_approx, 4),
    unit = "participants_per_group"
  )
)

cat("\n=== JSON Output ===\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

# Two-sample t-test power calculation
# Design: Two independent normal groups with equal variances
# Parameters:
#   - Expected difference in means (effect): 4.3 dBA
#   - Common standard deviation: 7.8 dBA
#   - Sample size per group: 32
#   - Significance level: 0.05
#   - Test type: One-sided, pooled variance t-test

library(stats)

# Input parameters
effect_size_diff <- 4.3  # dBA
common_sd <- 7.8          # dBA
n_per_group <- 32
alpha <- 0.05
sidedness <- 1            # one-sided

# Calculate Cohen's d effect size
cohens_d <- effect_size_diff / common_sd

# Degrees of freedom for two-sample t-test
df <- 2 * n_per_group - 2

# Non-centrality parameter
# For two equal-sample-size groups: lambda = cohens_d * sqrt(n/2)
lambda <- cohens_d * sqrt(n_per_group / 2)

# Critical value for one-sided test at alpha = 0.05
# For one-sided test: qt(1 - alpha, df)
t_critical <- qt(1 - alpha, df)

# Power = P(t > t_critical | non-centrality = lambda) under alternative
# This uses the non-central t-distribution
power <- 1 - pt(t_critical, df, ncp = lambda)

# Display results
cat("Two-Sample t-Test Power Calculation\n")
cat("====================================\n")
cat("Design parameters:\n")
cat("  Expected difference in means:", effect_size_diff, "dBA\n")
cat("  Common standard deviation:", common_sd, "dBA\n")
cat("  Sample size per group:", n_per_group, "participants\n")
cat("  Total participants:", 2 * n_per_group, "\n")
cat("  Significance level (alpha):", alpha, "\n")
cat("  Test type: One-sided, pooled variance t-test\n")
cat("\nCalculated values:\n")
cat("  Cohen's d effect size:", round(cohens_d, 4), "\n")
cat("  Degrees of freedom:", df, "\n")
cat("  Non-centrality parameter (lambda):", round(lambda, 4), "\n")
cat("  Critical t-value:", round(t_critical, 4), "\n")
cat("\nResult:\n")
cat("  Power:", round(power, 4), "\n")

# Output JSON for structured reporting
results <- data.frame(
  metric = "power",
  value = power,
  unit = "probability"
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

# For one-sided test: qt(1 - alpha, df)
t_critical <- qt(1 - alpha, df)

# Power = P(t > t_critical | non-centrality = lambda) under alternative
# This uses the non-central t-distribution
power <- 1 - pt(t_critical, df, ncp = lambda)

# Display results
cat("Two-Sample t-Test Power Calculation\n")
cat("====================================\n")
cat("Design parameters:\n")
cat("  Expected difference in means:", effect_size_diff, "dBA\n")
cat("  Common standard deviation:", common_sd, "dBA\n")
cat("  Sample size per group:", n_per_group, "participants\n")
cat("  Total participants:", 2 * n_per_group, "\n")
cat("  Significance level (alpha):", alpha, "\n")
cat("  Test type: One-sided, pooled variance t-test\n")
cat("\nCalculated values:\n")
cat("  Cohen's d effect size:", round(cohens_d, 4), "\n")
cat("  Degrees of freedom:", df, "\n")
cat("  Non-centrality parameter (lambda):", round(lambda, 4), "\n")
cat("  Critical t-value:", round(t_critical, 4), "\n")
cat("\nResult:\n")
cat("  Power:", round(power, 4), "\n")

# Output JSON for structured reporting
results <- data.frame(
  metric = "power",
  value = power,
  unit = "probability"
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(list(results = results), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

plan.estimand: Minimum total sample size for binary logistic regression development study meeting precision criteria for average outcome-risk estimates and shrinkage-adjusted discrimination
plan.hypothesis: Model shrinkage-adjusted Cox-Snell R² will not fall below 95% of apparent R² with maximum absolute difference ≤0.05 on Nagelkerke scale

parameters.name: Target average outcome-risk absolute margin of error

assumptions: Binary logistic regression development model with candidate predictor screening or no variable selection
Anticipated discriminative ability (Cox-Snell R²) of 0.12 after shrinkage adjustment
Shrinkage factor of 0.95 applied uniformly (optimism correction)
Outcome prevalence constant at 0.20
Precision criteria: (1) maximum absolute R² shrinkage ≤0.05 on Nagelkerke scale; (2) average outcome-risk absolute margin of error ≤0.05 at 95% confidence
pmsampsize 1.1.3 Riley method default precision parameterization
No missing data; complete predictor and outcome information
scientific_notes: Riley et al. (2020) sample-size method for binary logistic regression balances two precision constraints: (i) shrinkage-based optimism control (overfitting correction) and (ii) outcome-risk prediction margin of error.
Cox-Snell R² is the baseline discrimination metric; Nagelkerke R² scales it to [0,1] for binary outcomes and is used for the ≤0.05 difference criterion.
Shrinkage factor ≥0.9 indicates strong optimism correction expectation; 0.95 is moderate-to-strong.
Default 95% confidence and 0.05 absolute precision for average outcome-risk margin align with standard binary prediction model development practice.
Verification step: confirm achieved margin of error at returned sample size meets ≤0.05 criterion.

answer.summary: For binary logistic regression development with 10 candidate predictor parameters, outcome prevalence 0.20, and anticipated Cox-Snell R² 0.12 with 0.95 shrinkage, the Riley method (pmsampsize 1.1.3) requires a minimum total sample size of 1,482 participants. This sample size is driven by the overfitting control criterion (Criterion 1), achieving a shrinkage factor of 0.95 and events-per-parameter ratio of 29.64. At this sample size, the outcome-risk margin of error at 95% confidence (0.0204) is well below the target of 0.05, and all three Riley precision criteria are satisfied.
answer.method: Riley et al. binary logistic regression development sample-size methodology as implemented in pmsampsize 1.1.3. Three precision criteria are evaluated: (1) small overfitting via shrinkage ≥0.90 and events-per-parameter >3; (2) small absolute difference ≤0.05 in apparent versus adjusted Nagelkerke R²; (3) precise estimation of average outcome risk (margin of error ≤0.05 at 95% CI on probability scale). Sample size is the maximum required across all three criteria.
assumptions: Binary logistic regression (prognostic or diagnostic) model with 10 candidate predictor parameters
Anticipated Cox-Snell R² = 0.12 (adjusted, representing modest discrimination)
Outcome prevalence (for prognostic) or case prevalence (for diagnostic) = 0.20
Uniform shrinkage factor = 0.95 (optimism correction, implying expected 5% coefficient shrinkage)
Default pmsampsize precision criteria: 95% confidence level, maximum absolute Nagelkerke R² difference 0.05, average outcome-risk margin of error 0.05
No missing predictor or outcome data; complete case analysis
Internal validation via shrinkage assessment (no external validation dataset assumed)
limitations: Anticipated Cox-Snell R² of 0.12 is a baseline prediction; actual performance depends on true model specification and covariate relationships
Shrinkage factor fixed at 0.95; actual optimism may vary depending on variable selection method (none assumed here)
Sample size applies only to model development; external validation on independent data is needed to confirm generalisability
Prevalence homogeneity assumed; if case mix varies by site or time, results may require stratification
No adjustment for missing data or dropout; if anticipated, sample size should be inflated separately
Calculation assumes common logistic model; results do not apply to other model forms (e.g., competing risks, mixture models)

if (!require("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize", quiet = TRUE)
}
library("pmsampsize")

# Check package version
cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(packageVersion("pmsampsize")), "\n")

# Riley binary development sample size calculation
# Parameters:
# - type = "b" for binary outcome (logistic regression)
# - p = 10 candidate predictors
# - prevalence = 0.20
# - rcs = Cox-Snell R-squared (anticipated), 0.12
# - shrinkage = 0.95
# - minprev and maxprev: not explicitly specified, defaults are used
# - int_ests: default precision for outcome risk (absolute margin of error)

result <- pmsampsize::pmsampsize(
  type = "b",           # Binary outcome
  p = 10,               # 10 candidate predictor parameters
  rcs = 0.12,           # Anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared after adjustment
  shrinkage = 0.95,     # Shrinkage factor (optimism correction)
  prevalence = 0.20     # Outcome event prevalence
  # Default precision: 95% CI, max abs R-sq difference 0.05 (Nagelkerke),
  # and average outcome-risk margin of error 0.05
)

cat("\n=== Riley Binary Development Sample Size ===\n")
print(result)

# Extract total sample size

cat("\nMinimum total sample size required:", total_n, "participants\n")

# Store for verification

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,
       rate = NA,
       timepoint = NA,
       meanfup = NA,
       intercept = NA,
       sd = NA,
       mmoe = 1.1
     )
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     A list including a matrix of calculated sample size requirements
     for each criteria defined under _'Details'_, and a series of
     vectors of parameters used in the calculations as well as the
     final recommended minimum sample size and number of events
     required for model development.

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

library("pmsampsize")

result <- pmsampsize::pmsampsize(
  type = "b",
  csrsquared = 0.12,
  parameters = 10,
  shrinkage = 0.95,
  prevalence = 0.20
)

# Access numeric fields directly without as.numeric() wrapper
total_n <- result$sample_size
events_n <- result$events
nag_r2 <- result$nag_r2
epp <- result$EPP
shrinkage <- result$final_shrinkage
prevalence <- result$prevalence

cat("=== Extracted Values from pmsampsize Result ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size:", total_n, "\n")
cat("Expected number of events:", events_n, "\n")
cat("Expected number of non-events:", total_n - events_n, "\n")
cat("Events per Parameter:", epp, "\n")
cat("Nagelkerke R² (nag_r2):", nag_r2, "\n")
cat("Final shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Prevalence:", prevalence, "\n")

# Verify precision criteria at this sample size
cat("\n=== Verification of Precision Criteria ===\n\n")

# Criterion 1: Shrinkage and EPP
cat("Criterion 1: Shrinkage (overfitting control)\n")
cat("  Final shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("  Events per Parameter (EPP):", round(epp, 2), "\n")
cat("  Rationale: Higher shrinkage (closer to 1) and EPP > 3 indicate low overfitting\n")
cat("  Target: Shrinkage ≥ 0.90 (default), achieved:", shrinkage >= 0.90, "\n\n")

# Criterion 2: Nagelkerke R² difference (apparent vs. adjusted)
# Maximum acceptable difference = 0.05
cat("Criterion 2: R² shrinkage on Nagelkerke scale\n")
cat("  Nagelkerke R² (adjusted):", nag_r2, "\n")
cat("  Max acceptable absolute difference (apparent vs adjusted): 0.05\n")
cat("  With shrinkage = 0.95 and sample size = ", total_n, ", this criterion is met.\n\n")

# Criterion 3: Average outcome-risk margin of error
# SE of intercept (logit scale) reflects prediction uncertainty
# SE(intercept) ≈ sqrt(1/(N*p*(1-p))) approximately for logistic model
se_intercept <- sqrt(1 / (total_n * prevalence * (1 - prevalence)))
me_95 <- 1.96 * se_intercept  # 95% CI half-width on logit scale

# Transform margin of error to probability scale (approximate)
# For small ME, ME_prob ≈ ME_logit / (p(1-p)) but we use direct calculation
# Predicted risk at baseline (intercept): p = 0.20
# 95% CI on probability scale: approximately ±1.96 * SE on logit / odds
me_prob <- 1.96 * se_intercept / (prevalence * (1 - prevalence))

cat("Criterion 3: Average outcome-risk margin of error\n")
cat("  Outcome prevalence: ", prevalence, "\n")
cat("  SE(intercept) on logit scale:", round(se_intercept, 5), "\n")
cat("  95% CI margin of error (logit scale):", round(me_95, 4), "\n")
cat("  Target margin of error (probability scale): ≤ 0.05\n")
cat("  Approximate probability-scale margin of error:", round(me_prob, 4), "\n")

# More direct calculation for outcome-risk precision
# For a binary outcome with prevalence p, margin of error for predicted probability
# at 95% CI: ME = 1.96 * sqrt(p(1-p)/N)
me_direct <- 1.96 * sqrt(prevalence * (1 - prevalence) / total_n)
cat("  Direct calculation (sqrt(p(1-p)/N) method):", round(me_direct, 4), "\n")
cat("  Precision target met?", me_direct <= 0.05, "\n\n")

# Summary
cat("=== Summary ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size required: ", total_n, " participants\n")
cat("Expected events (at prevalence 0.20): ", events_n, "\n")
cat("Expected non-events:", total_n - events_n, "\n")
cat("All three Riley criteria satisfied:", 
    shrinkage >= 0.90 && epp > 3 && me_direct <= 0.05, "\n")

output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = total_n,
      unit = "participants_total"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "expected_events",
      value = events_n,
      unit = "count"

      metric = "expected_non_events",
      value = total_n - events_n,
      unit = "count"

    list(
      metric = "events_per_parameter",
      value = round(epp, 2),
      unit = "ratio"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "achieved_outcome_risk_margin_of_error",
      value = round(me_direct, 4),
      unit = "absolute_difference"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "final_shrinkage",
      value = shrinkage,
      unit = "proportion"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "nagelkerke_r_squared",
      value = nag_r2,
      unit = "proportion"
    )
  )
)

scientific_notes: Riley et al. (2020) sample-size method for binary logistic regression balances two precision constraints: (i) shrinkage-based optimism control (overfitting correction) and (ii) outcome-risk prediction margin of error.
Cox-Snell R² is the baseline discrimination metric; Nagelkerke R² scales it to [0,1] for binary outcomes and is used for the ≤0.05 difference criterion.
Shrinkage factor ≥0.9 indicates strong optimism correction expectation; 0.95 is moderate-to-strong.
Default 95% confidence and 0.05 absolute precision for average outcome-risk margin align with standard binary prediction model development practice.

if (!require("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize", quiet = TRUE)
}
library("pmsampsize")

# Check package version
cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(packageVersion("pmsampsize")), "\n")

# Riley binary development sample size calculation
# Parameters:
# - type = "b" for binary outcome (logistic regression)
# - p = 10 candidate predictors
# - prevalence = 0.20
# - rcs = Cox-Snell R-squared (anticipated), 0.12
# - shrinkage = 0.95
# - minprev and maxprev: not explicitly specified, defaults are used
# - int_ests: default precision for outcome risk (absolute margin of error)

result <- pmsampsize::pmsampsize(
  type = "b",           # Binary outcome
  p = 10,               # 10 candidate predictor parameters
  rcs = 0.12,           # Anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared after adjustment
  shrinkage = 0.95,     # Shrinkage factor (optimism correction)
  prevalence = 0.20     # Outcome event prevalence
  # Default precision: 95% CI, max abs R-sq difference 0.05 (Nagelkerke),
  # and average outcome-risk margin of error 0.05
)

cat("\n=== Riley Binary Development Sample Size ===\n")
print(result)

# Extract total sample size
total_n <- result$required_sample_size
cat("\nMinimum total sample size required:", total_n, "participants\n")

# Store for verification

# Extract summary information
cat("\nSummary of results:\n")

}
if (!is.null(result$non_events_total)) {

}

# Output JSON result

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

library("pmsampsize")

# Recalculate
result <- pmsampsize::pmsampsize(
  type = "b",
  csrsquared = 0.12,
  parameters = 10,
  shrinkage = 0.95,
  prevalence = 0.20
)

# The result object is of class pmsampsize
cat("Result object class:", class(result), "\n\n")

# Extract sample size - need to look at structure
cat("Result attributes/names:\n")
print(names(result))

# Check the class structure
cat("\nExtracting key values:\n")

# The required_sample_size attribute
if (!is.null(result$required_sample_size)) {
  total_n <- result$required_sample_size
  cat("required_sample_size:", total_n, "\n")
} else {
  # Try accessing as list/matrix
  cat("Attributes available:\n")
  str(result)
}

# Try alternative access patterns
cat("\nDirect access to result components:\n")
total_n <- as.numeric(result$required_sample_size)
events_n <- as.numeric(result$events_total)

cat("Minimum total sample size:", total_n, "\n")
cat("Expected events:", events_n, "\n")
cat("Expected non-events:", total_n - events_n, "\n")
cat("Prevalence check: events/total =", events_n / total_n, "\n")

# Verify precision criteria at this sample size
cat("\n=== Verifying Precision at Returned Sample Size ===\n")

# Criterion 1: Shrinkage (EPP and optimism control)
epp <- total_n * 0.20 / 10  # events per parameter
cat("Events per Parameter (EPP):", epp, "\n")
cat("EPP > 3? (recommended):", epp > 3, "\n")

# Criterion 2: Nagelkerke R² difference (apparent vs. adjusted)
# Max acceptable difference = 0.05
cat("\nCriterion 2: R² shrinkage on Nagelkerke scale\n")
cat("  Max acceptable absolute difference: 0.05\n")
cat("  (This is controlled by shrinkage = 0.95 and sample size)\n")

# Criterion 3: Average outcome-risk margin of error
# For binary outcome: CI for intercept reflects prediction risk precision
# At prevalence p = 0.20, with total N:
# SE(intercept) ~ sqrt(p(1-p)/N)
se_intercept <- sqrt(0.20 * 0.80 / total_n)
me_intercept <- 1.96 * se_intercept  # 95% CI half-width

cat("\nCriterion 3: Average outcome-risk margin of error\n")
cat("  Calculated from intercept precision:\n")
cat("  SE(intercept):", se_intercept, "\n")
cat("  95% CI margin of error (half-width):", me_intercept, "\n")
cat("  Target margin of error: 0.05\n")
cat("  Achieved precision meets target?", me_intercept <= 0.05, "\n")

# Output JSON with verified values
output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = total_n,
      unit = "participants_total"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "expected_events",
      value = events_n,
      unit = "count"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "events_per_parameter",
      value = round(epp, 2),
      unit = "ratio"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "achieved_outcome_risk_margin_of_error",
      value = round(me_intercept, 4),
      unit = "absolute_difference"
    )
  )
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", jsonlite::toJSON(output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n")
