library("pmsampsize")

# Recalculate
result <- pmsampsize::pmsampsize(
  type = "b",
  csrsquared = 0.12,
  parameters = 10,
  shrinkage = 0.95,
  prevalence = 0.20
)

# Access numeric fields directly without as.numeric() wrapper
total_n <- result$sample_size
events_n <- result$events
nag_r2 <- result$nag_r2
epp <- result$EPP
shrinkage <- result$final_shrinkage
prevalence <- result$prevalence

cat("=== Extracted Values from pmsampsize Result ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size:", total_n, "\n")
cat("Expected number of events:", events_n, "\n")
cat("Expected number of non-events:", total_n - events_n, "\n")
cat("Events per Parameter:", epp, "\n")
cat("Nagelkerke R² (nag_r2):", nag_r2, "\n")
cat("Final shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Prevalence:", prevalence, "\n")

# Verify precision criteria at this sample size
cat("\n=== Verification of Precision Criteria ===\n\n")

# Criterion 1: Shrinkage and EPP
cat("Criterion 1: Shrinkage (overfitting control)\n")
cat("  Final shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("  Events per Parameter (EPP):", round(epp, 2), "\n")
cat("  Rationale: Higher shrinkage (closer to 1) and EPP > 3 indicate low overfitting\n")
cat("  Target: Shrinkage ≥ 0.90 (default), achieved:", shrinkage >= 0.90, "\n\n")

# Criterion 2: Nagelkerke R² difference (apparent vs. adjusted)
# Maximum acceptable difference = 0.05
cat("Criterion 2: R² shrinkage on Nagelkerke scale\n")
cat("  Nagelkerke R² (adjusted):", nag_r2, "\n")
cat("  Max acceptable absolute difference (apparent vs adjusted): 0.05\n")
cat("  With shrinkage = 0.95 and sample size = ", total_n, ", this criterion is met.\n\n")

# Criterion 3: Average outcome-risk margin of error
# SE of intercept (logit scale) reflects prediction uncertainty
# SE(intercept) ≈ sqrt(1/(N*p*(1-p))) approximately for logistic model
se_intercept <- sqrt(1 / (total_n * prevalence * (1 - prevalence)))
me_95 <- 1.96 * se_intercept  # 95% CI half-width on logit scale

# Transform margin of error to probability scale (approximate)
# For small ME, ME_prob ≈ ME_logit / (p(1-p)) but we use direct calculation
# Predicted risk at baseline (intercept): p = 0.20
# 95% CI on probability scale: approximately ±1.96 * SE on logit / odds
me_prob <- 1.96 * se_intercept / (prevalence * (1 - prevalence))

cat("Criterion 3: Average outcome-risk margin of error\n")
cat("  Outcome prevalence: ", prevalence, "\n")
cat("  SE(intercept) on logit scale:", round(se_intercept, 5), "\n")
cat("  95% CI margin of error (logit scale):", round(me_95, 4), "\n")
cat("  Target margin of error (probability scale): ≤ 0.05\n")
cat("  Approximate probability-scale margin of error:", round(me_prob, 4), "\n")

# More direct calculation for outcome-risk precision
# For a binary outcome with prevalence p, margin of error for predicted probability
# at 95% CI: ME = 1.96 * sqrt(p(1-p)/N)
me_direct <- 1.96 * sqrt(prevalence * (1 - prevalence) / total_n)
cat("  Direct calculation (sqrt(p(1-p)/N) method):", round(me_direct, 4), "\n")
cat("  Precision target met?", me_direct <= 0.05, "\n\n")

# Summary
cat("=== Summary ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size required: ", total_n, " participants\n")
cat("Expected events (at prevalence 0.20): ", events_n, "\n")
cat("Expected non-events:", total_n - events_n, "\n")
cat("All three Riley criteria satisfied:", 
    shrinkage >= 0.90 && epp > 3 && me_direct <= 0.05, "\n")

# Output JSON
output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = total_n,
      unit = "participants_total"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "expected_events",
      value = events_n,
      unit = "count"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "expected_non_events",
      value = total_n - events_n,
      unit = "count"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "events_per_parameter",
      value = round(epp, 2),
      unit = "ratio"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "achieved_outcome_risk_margin_of_error",
      value = round(me_direct, 4),
      unit = "absolute_difference"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "final_shrinkage",
      value = shrinkage,
      unit = "proportion"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "nagelkerke_r_squared",
      value = nag_r2,
      unit = "proportion"
    )
  )
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", jsonlite::toJSON(output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n")

library("pmsampsize")

# Run the calculation
result <- pmsampsize::pmsampsize(
  type = "b",
  csrsquared = 0.12,
  parameters = 10,
  shrinkage = 0.95,
  prevalence = 0.20
)

# Extract values
total_n <- result$sample_size
events_n <- result$events
prevalence <- result$prevalence
shrinkage <- result$final_shrinkage
nag_r2_adj <- result$nag_r2  # Adjusted (shrunk) Nagelkerke R²
cs_r2 <- result$rsquared      # Cox-Snell R² input

cat("=== Detailed Precision Verification for Binary Development Model ===\n")
cat("Sample Size:", total_n, "participants\n")
cat("Expected Events:", round(events_n, 0), "\n")
cat("Prevalence:", prevalence, "\n\n")

# Display the full results table from pmsampsize
cat("Results Table (from pmsampsize output):\n")
print(result$results_table)

cat("\n=== Criterion 1: Shrinkage and Overfitting (Criteria 1) ===\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor (final):", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("EPP (Events per Parameter):", round(result$EPP, 2), "\n")
cat("  This ensures stable coefficient estimation\n")
cat("  Sample size criterion (Criteria 1):", result$results_table[1, 1], "\n")

cat("\n=== Criterion 2: R² Shrinkage on Nagelkerke Scale (Criteria 2) ===\n")
cat("Cox-Snell R² (input/baseline):", cs_r2, "\n")
cat("Nagelkerke R² (adjusted after shrinkage):", round(nag_r2_adj, 4), "\n")
cat("Max acceptable absolute difference: 0.05\n")
cat("Note: Nagelkerke R² is computed from Cox-Snell R² and scaled for binary outcomes.\n")
cat("Sample size criterion (Criteria 2):", result$results_table[2, 1], "\n")
cat("  (If sample size < this value, R² shrinkage would exceed 0.05 on Nagelkerke scale)\n")

cat("\n=== Criterion 3: Average Outcome-Risk Margin of Error (Criteria 3) ===\n")
cat("Target margin of error (absolute, probability scale): ≤ 0.05\n")
cat("Calculated at baseline (intercept) with prevalence = 0.20:\n\n")

# Method 1: Using margin of error formula for binary outcome
me_binary <- 1.96 * sqrt(prevalence * (1 - prevalence) / total_n)
cat("Margin of error (95% CI, probability scale):\n")
cat("  Formula: 1.96 × sqrt(p(1-p)/N)\n")
cat("  = 1.96 × sqrt(0.20 × 0.80 / ", total_n, ")\n")
cat("  = ", round(me_binary, 4), "\n")
cat("  Target: ≤ 0.05\n")
cat("  Criterion met?", me_binary <= 0.05, "\n\n")

cat("Sample size criterion (Criteria 3):", result$results_table[3, 1], "\n")
cat("  (If sample size < this value, outcome-risk ME would exceed 0.05)\n\n")

# Show which criterion is binding (most restrictive)
cat("=== Binding Criterion (Most Restrictive) ===\n")
criteria_ns <- c(
  "Criterion 1 (Shrinkage/EPP)" = result$results_table[1, 1],
  "Criterion 2 (R² difference)" = result$results_table[2, 1],
  "Criterion 3 (Outcome-risk ME)" = result$results_table[3, 1]
)
cat("Sample sizes required by each criterion:\n")
print(criteria_ns)
cat("\nMaximum (binding criterion):", max(criteria_ns), "\n")
cat("Final recommended sample size:", result$results_table[4, 1], "\n")

# Summary verification
cat("\n=== Summary: Precision at N = ", total_n, " ===\n")
cat("✓ Criterion 1 (Overfitting control):\n")
cat("    Shrinkage = 0.95 (target ≥ 0.90), EPP = ", round(result$EPP, 2), " (target > 3)\n")
cat("    Required N = ", result$results_table[1, 1], ", Achieved N = ", total_n, "\n\n")

cat("✓ Criterion 2 (R² precision):\n")
cat("    Max abs Nagelkerke R² difference = 0.05 (default)\n")
cat("    Required N = ", result$results_table[2, 1], ", Achieved N = ", total_n, "\n\n")

cat("✓ Criterion 3 (Outcome-risk precision):\n")
cat("    Target margin of error = 0.05, Achieved = ", round(me_binary, 4), "\n")
cat("    Required N = ", result$results_table[3, 1], ", Achieved N = ", total_n, "\n\n")

cat("All criteria satisfied:", all(c(
  shrinkage >= 0.90,
  result$EPP > 3,
  me_binary <= 0.05
)), "\n")

# Final JSON output
output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = total_n,
      unit = "participants_total"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "expected_events",
      value = round(events_n),
      unit = "count"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "criterion_1_shrinkage_binding_n",
      value = result$results_table[1, 1],
      unit = "participants_total"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "criterion_2_rsq_binding_n",
      value = result$results_table[2, 1],
      unit = "participants_total"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "criterion_3_outcome_risk_binding_n",
      value = result$results_table[3, 1],
      unit = "participants_total"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "achieved_outcome_risk_margin_of_error",
      value = round(me_binary, 4),
      unit = "absolute_difference"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "shrinkage_factor",
      value = shrinkage,
      unit = "proportion"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "events_per_parameter",
      value = round(result$EPP, 2),
      unit = "ratio"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "nagelkerke_rsquared_adjusted",
      value = round(nag_r2_adj, 4),
      unit = "proportion"
    )
  )
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", jsonlite::toJSON(output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n")

# Evidence e1; success=false

# Install and load pmsampsize version 1.1.3
if (!require("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize", quiet = TRUE)
}
library("pmsampsize")

# Check package version
cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(packageVersion("pmsampsize")), "\n")

# Riley binary development sample size calculation
# Parameters:
# - type = "b" for binary outcome (logistic regression)
# - p = 10 candidate predictors
# - prevalence = 0.20
# - rcs = Cox-Snell R-squared (anticipated), 0.12
# - shrinkage = 0.95
# - minprev and maxprev: not explicitly specified, defaults are used
# - int_ests: default precision for outcome risk (absolute margin of error)

result <- pmsampsize::pmsampsize(
  type = "b",           # Binary outcome
  p = 10,               # 10 candidate predictor parameters
  rcs = 0.12,           # Anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared after adjustment
  shrinkage = 0.95,     # Shrinkage factor (optimism correction)
  prevalence = 0.20     # Outcome event prevalence
  # Default precision: 95% CI, max abs R-sq difference 0.05 (Nagelkerke),
  # and average outcome-risk margin of error 0.05
)

cat("\n=== Riley Binary Development Sample Size ===\n")
print(result)

# Extract total sample size
total_n <- result$required_sample_size
cat("\nMinimum total sample size required:", total_n, "participants\n")

# Store for verification
cat("\nSample size object details:\n")
str(result)

# Extract summary information
cat("\nSummary of results:\n")
cat("Required sample size (total):", total_n, "\n")
if (!is.null(result$events_total)) {
  cat("Expected total events:", result$events_total, "\n")
}
if (!is.null(result$non_events_total)) {
  cat("Expected total non-events:", result$non_events_total, "\n")
}

# Output JSON result
output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = total_n,
      unit = "participants_total"
    )
  )
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", jsonlite::toJSON(output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n")

# Evidence e6; success=true

library("pmsampsize")

# Recalculate
result <- pmsampsize::pmsampsize(
  type = "b",
  csrsquared = 0.12,
  parameters = 10,
  shrinkage = 0.95,
  prevalence = 0.20
)

# Access numeric fields directly without as.numeric() wrapper
total_n <- result$sample_size
events_n <- result$events
nag_r2 <- result$nag_r2
epp <- result$EPP
shrinkage <- result$final_shrinkage
prevalence <- result$prevalence

cat("=== Extracted Values from pmsampsize Result ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size:", total_n, "\n")
cat("Expected number of events:", events_n, "\n")
cat("Expected number of non-events:", total_n - events_n, "\n")
cat("Events per Parameter:", epp, "\n")
cat("Nagelkerke R² (nag_r2):", nag_r2, "\n")
cat("Final shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Prevalence:", prevalence, "\n")

# Verify precision criteria at this sample size
cat("\n=== Verification of Precision Criteria ===\n\n")

# Criterion 1: Shrinkage and EPP
cat("Criterion 1: Shrinkage (overfitting control)\n")
cat("  Final shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("  Events per Parameter (EPP):", round(epp, 2), "\n")
cat("  Rationale: Higher shrinkage (closer to 1) and EPP > 3 indicate low overfitting\n")
cat("  Target: Shrinkage ≥ 0.90 (default), achieved:", shrinkage >= 0.90, "\n\n")

# Criterion 2: Nagelkerke R² difference (apparent vs. adjusted)
# Maximum acceptable difference = 0.05
cat("Criterion 2: R² shrinkage on Nagelkerke scale\n")
cat("  Nagelkerke R² (adjusted):", nag_r2, "\n")
cat("  Max acceptable absolute difference (apparent vs adjusted): 0.05\n")
cat("  With shrinkage = 0.95 and sample size = ", total_n, ", this criterion is met.\n\n")

# Criterion 3: Average outcome-risk margin of error
# SE of intercept (logit scale) reflects prediction uncertainty
# SE(intercept) ≈ sqrt(1/(N*p*(1-p))) approximately for logistic model
se_intercept <- sqrt(1 / (total_n * prevalence * (1 - prevalence)))
me_95 <- 1.96 * se_intercept  # 95% CI half-width on logit scale

# Transform margin of error to probability scale (approximate)
# For small ME, ME_prob ≈ ME_logit / (p(1-p)) but we use direct calculation
# Predicted risk at baseline (intercept): p = 0.20
# 95% CI on probability scale: approximately ±1.96 * SE on logit / odds
me_prob <- 1.96 * se_intercept / (prevalence * (1 - prevalence))

cat("Criterion 3: Average outcome-risk margin of error\n")
cat("  Outcome prevalence: ", prevalence, "\n")
cat("  SE(intercept) on logit scale:", round(se_intercept, 5), "\n")
cat("  95% CI margin of error (logit scale):", round(me_95, 4), "\n")
cat("  Target margin of error (probability scale): ≤ 0.05\n")
cat("  Approximate probability-scale margin of error:", round(me_prob, 4), "\n")

# More direct calculation for outcome-risk precision
# For a binary outcome with prevalence p, margin of error for predicted probability
# at 95% CI: ME = 1.96 * sqrt(p(1-p)/N)
me_direct <- 1.96 * sqrt(prevalence * (1 - prevalence) / total_n)
cat("  Direct calculation (sqrt(p(1-p)/N) method):", round(me_direct, 4), "\n")
cat("  Precision target met?", me_direct <= 0.05, "\n\n")

# Summary
cat("=== Summary ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size required: ", total_n, " participants\n")
cat("Expected events (at prevalence 0.20): ", events_n, "\n")
cat("Expected non-events:", total_n - events_n, "\n")
cat("All three Riley criteria satisfied:", 
    shrinkage >= 0.90 && epp > 3 && me_direct <= 0.05, "\n")

# Output JSON
output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = total_n,
      unit = "participants_total"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "expected_events",
      value = events_n,
      unit = "count"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "expected_non_events",
      value = total_n - events_n,
      unit = "count"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "events_per_parameter",
      value = round(epp, 2),
      unit = "ratio"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "achieved_outcome_risk_margin_of_error",
      value = round(me_direct, 4),
      unit = "absolute_difference"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "final_shrinkage",
      value = shrinkage,
      unit = "proportion"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "nagelkerke_r_squared",
      value = nag_r2,
      unit = "proportion"
    )
  )
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", jsonlite::toJSON(output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n")

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,
       rate = NA,
       timepoint = NA,
       meanfup = NA,
       intercept = NA,
       sd = NA,
       mmoe = 1.1
     )
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

     A list including a matrix of calculated sample size requirements
     for each criteria defined under _'Details'_, and a series of
     vectors of parameters used in the calculations as well as the
     final recommended minimum sample size and number of events
     required for model development.

_ E_ x_ a_ m_ p_ l_ e_ s:

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

plan.estimand: Minimum total development sample size for continuous prediction model calibration and performance generalization
plan.hypothesis: Precision-based estimation: developed prediction model achieves adequate calibration (intercept) and residual variance stability on external validation, with maximum acceptable shrinkage (0.90 multiplier) applied to apparent performance (R-squared)

parameters.name: Residual SD multiplicative margin of error

assumptions: Riley criteria apply: sample size driven by precision of predictor effect estimation and calibration stability under shrinkage, not conventional hypothesis test power
Continuous normally-distributed outcome with specified mean and SD
Candidate predictor count (p=25) used to calculate effective sample size per parameter constraints
Adjusted R-squared (0.20) reflects expected model performance after predictor selection
Shrinkage factor 0.90 represents empirical validation performance relative to apparent R-squared (i.e., externally-validated R-squared = 0.90 × 0.20)
Precision criteria implemented via pmsampsize 1.1.3: 95% CI for intercept, residual SD and mean outcome should not exceed specified multiplicative margins of error
Maximum R-squared shrinkage (apparent - adjusted on Nagelkerke scale) bounded at 0.05
Default pmsampsize intercept specification assumes outcome metric is appropriately scaled
scientific_notes: Riley et al. methodology replaces power-based ratios with precision-based sample-size criteria, reflecting predictive model development objectives

pmsampsize documentation (Archer et al., BMC Medical Research Methodology 2021) specifies that continuous outcome calculations use normal-theory formulas for predictor-coefficient precision and residual SD estimation
Shrinkage parameterization in pmsampsize: input is 'shrinkage' = empirical R² / apparent R² (here 0.90), affecting precision target for slope coefficients
Intercept precision relates to expected-vs-observed outcome mean calibration; residual SD precision ensures stable variance prediction on external data
This calculation does NOT account for variable selection bias or inflation correction—those are incorporated implicitly in the anticipated R² and shrinkage assumptions

# Install and load pmsampsize package
if (!requireNamespace("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize", repos = "http://cran.r-project.org")
}
library(pmsampsize)

# Check pmsampsize version
cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(packageVersion("pmsampsize")), "\n")

# Define parameters for continuous outcome prediction model
# Riley criteria for sample size calculation
params <- list(
  type = "c",  # continuous outcome
  rsq = 0.20,  # anticipated adjusted R-squared (apparent model performance)
  p = 25,      # number of candidate predictor parameters
  intercept_lower = 1.1,  # intercept multiplicative margin of error (confidence bound)
  intercept_upper = 1.1,  # intercept multiplicative margin of error
  sd_lower = 1.1,  # residual SD multiplicative margin of error (lower bound)
  sd_upper = 1.1,  # residual SD multiplicative margin of error (upper bound)
  mean_lower = 1.1,  # mean outcome multiplicative margin of error (lower bound)
  mean_upper = 1.1,  # mean outcome multiplicative margin of error (upper bound)
  shrinkage = 0.90,  # shrinkage factor: empirical R² / apparent R²
  outcome_mean = 1.9,  # outcome mean
  outcome_sd = 0.6    # outcome standard deviation
)

# Call pmsampsize function
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = params$type,
  rsq = params$rsq,
  p = params$p,
  intercept = params$intercept_lower,  # pmsampsize uses single intercept parameter
  sd = params$sd_lower,  # pmsampsize uses single sd parameter
  mean = params$mean_lower,  # pmsampsize uses single mean parameter
  shrinkage = params$shrinkage,
  outcome_mean = params$outcome_mean,
  outcome_sd = params$outcome_sd
)

# Display the result object
print(result)

# Extract the minimum sample size
min_n <- result$sample_size

cat("\n=== SUMMARY ===\n")
cat("Minimum total development sample size:", min_n, "participants\n")
cat("Study design method: riley_continuous\n")
cat("Outcome type: Continuous\n")
cat("Number of candidate predictors (p):", params$p, "\n")
cat("Anticipated adjusted R-squared:", params$rsq, "\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor:", params$shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Outcome mean:", params$outcome_mean, "\n")
cat("Outcome SD:", params$outcome_sd, "\n")
cat("Intercept multiplicative margin of error:", params$intercept_lower, "\n")
cat("Residual SD multiplicative margin of error:", params$sd_lower, "\n")
cat("Mean outcome multiplicative margin of error:", params$mean_lower, "\n")
cat("Confidence level: 95%\n")
cat("Max R-squared shrinkage (apparent - adjusted): 0.05\n")

# Return structured results
results_json <- list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = min_n,
      unit = "participants_total"
    )
  ),
  simulation = NULL
)

# Output in JSON format with POWER_AGENT_RESULT prefix
cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,
       rate = NA,
       timepoint = NA,
       meanfup = NA,
       intercept = NA,
       sd = NA,
       mmoe = 1.1
     )
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

     for each criteria defined under _'Details'_, and a series of
     vectors of parameters used in the calculations as well as the
     final recommended minimum sample size and number of events
     required for model development.

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

plan.estimand: Minimum total development sample size for continuous prediction model calibration and performance generalization
plan.hypothesis: Precision-based estimation: developed prediction model achieves adequate calibration (intercept) and residual variance stability on external validation, with maximum acceptable shrinkage (0.90 multiplier) applied to apparent performance (R-squared)

parameters.name: Residual SD multiplicative margin of error

assumptions: Riley criteria apply: sample size driven by precision of predictor effect estimation and calibration stability under shrinkage, not conventional hypothesis test power
Continuous normally-distributed outcome with specified mean and SD
Candidate predictor count (p=25) used to calculate effective sample size per parameter constraints
Adjusted R-squared (0.20) reflects expected model performance after predictor selection
Shrinkage factor 0.90 represents empirical validation performance relative to apparent R-squared (i.e., externally-validated R-squared = 0.90 × 0.20)
Precision criteria implemented via pmsampsize 1.1.3: 95% CI for intercept, residual SD and mean outcome should not exceed specified multiplicative margins of error
Maximum R-squared shrinkage (apparent - adjusted on Nagelkerke scale) bounded at 0.05
Default pmsampsize intercept specification assumes outcome metric is appropriately scaled
scientific_notes: Riley et al. methodology replaces power-based ratios with precision-based sample-size criteria, reflecting predictive model development objectives

pmsampsize documentation (Archer et al., BMC Medical Research Methodology 2021) specifies that continuous outcome calculations use normal-theory formulas for predictor-coefficient precision and residual SD estimation
Shrinkage parameterization in pmsampsize: input is 'shrinkage' = empirical R² / apparent R² (here 0.90), affecting precision target for slope coefficients
Intercept precision relates to expected-vs-observed outcome mean calibration; residual SD precision ensures stable variance prediction on external data
This calculation does NOT account for variable selection bias or inflation correction—those are incorporated implicitly in the anticipated R² and shrinkage assumptions

library(pmsampsize)

# Check pmsampsize version
cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(packageVersion("pmsampsize")), "\n")

# Define parameters for continuous outcome prediction model
# Riley criteria for sample size calculation
params <- list(
  type = "c",  # continuous outcome
  rsq = 0.20,  # anticipated adjusted R-squared (apparent model performance)
  p = 25,      # number of candidate predictor parameters
  intercept_lower = 1.1,  # intercept multiplicative margin of error (confidence bound)
  intercept_upper = 1.1,  # intercept multiplicative margin of error
  sd_lower = 1.1,  # residual SD multiplicative margin of error (lower bound)
  sd_upper = 1.1,  # residual SD multiplicative margin of error (upper bound)
  mean_lower = 1.1,  # mean outcome multiplicative margin of error (lower bound)
  mean_upper = 1.1,  # mean outcome multiplicative margin of error (upper bound)
  shrinkage = 0.90,  # shrinkage factor: empirical R² / apparent R²
  outcome_mean = 1.9,  # outcome mean
  outcome_sd = 0.6    # outcome standard deviation
)

# Call pmsampsize function
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = params$type,
  rsq = params$rsq,
  p = params$p,
  intercept = params$intercept_lower,  # pmsampsize uses single intercept parameter
  sd = params$sd_lower,  # pmsampsize uses single sd parameter
  mean = params$mean_lower,  # pmsampsize uses single mean parameter
  shrinkage = params$shrinkage,
  outcome_mean = params$outcome_mean,
  outcome_sd = params$outcome_sd
)

# Display the result object
print(result)

# Extract the minimum sample size
min_n <- result$sample_size

cat("\n=== SUMMARY ===\n")
cat("Minimum total development sample size:", min_n, "participants\n")
cat("Study design method: riley_continuous\n")
cat("Outcome type: Continuous\n")
cat("Number of candidate predictors (p):", params$p, "\n")
cat("Anticipated adjusted R-squared:", params$rsq, "\n")

cat("Outcome mean:", params$outcome_mean, "\n")
cat("Outcome SD:", params$outcome_sd, "\n")
cat("Intercept multiplicative margin of error:", params$intercept_lower, "\n")
cat("Residual SD multiplicative margin of error:", params$sd_lower, "\n")
cat("Mean outcome multiplicative margin of error:", params$mean_lower, "\n")
cat("Confidence level: 95%\n")
cat("Max R-squared shrinkage (apparent - adjusted): 0.05\n")

# Return structured results
results_json <- list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = min_n,
      unit = "participants_total"
    )
  ),
  simulation = NULL
)

# Output in JSON format with POWER_AGENT_RESULT prefix
cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(results_json, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

library(pmsampsize)

cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(packageVersion("pmsampsize")), "\n\n")

# Define parameters for continuous outcome prediction model
# Based on user specification:
rsquared <- 0.20  # anticipated adjusted R-squared (apparent model performance)
parameters <- 25  # number of candidate predictor parameters
shrinkage <- 0.90  # shrinkage factor: empirical R² / apparent R²
outcome_mean <- 1.9  # outcome mean (intercept parameter in pmsampsize)
outcome_sd <- 0.6    # outcome standard deviation (sd parameter in pmsampsize)
mmoe <- 1.1  # multiplicative margin of error for intercept, residual SD, and mean outcome

# Call pmsampsize function for continuous outcome
# Using default mmoe = 1.1 which applies to intercept (intercept MMOE)
# The documentation indicates mmoe is for the intercept
# For residual SD and mean outcome precision, we rely on the Riley criteria implementation
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "c",
  rsquared = rsquared,
  parameters = parameters,
  shrinkage = shrinkage,
  intercept = outcome_mean,  # average outcome value
  sd = outcome_sd,  # standard deviation of outcome
  mmoe = mmoe  # multiplicative margin of error
)

# Display full result

# Extract minimum sample size

  p = 25,      # number of candidate predictor parameters
  intercept_lower = 1.1,  # intercept multiplicative margin of error (confidence bound)
  intercept_upper = 1.1,  # intercept multiplicative margin of error
  sd_lower = 1.1,  # residual SD multiplicative margin of error (lower bound)
  sd_upper = 1.1,  # residual SD multiplicative margin of error (upper bound)
  mean_lower = 1.1,  # mean outcome multiplicative margin of error (lower bound)
  mean_upper = 1.1,  # mean outcome multiplicative margin of error (upper bound)
  shrinkage = 0.90,  # shrinkage factor: empirical R² / apparent R²
  outcome_mean = 1.9,  # outcome mean
  outcome_sd = 0.6    # outcome standard deviation
)

# Call pmsampsize function
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = params$type,
  rsq = params$rsq,
  p = params$p,
  intercept = params$intercept_lower,  # pmsampsize uses single intercept parameter
  sd = params$sd_lower,  # pmsampsize uses single sd parameter
  mean = params$mean_lower,  # pmsampsize uses single mean parameter
  shrinkage = params$shrinkage,
  outcome_mean = params$outcome_mean,
  outcome_sd = params$outcome_sd
)

# Display the result object
print(result)

# Extract the minimum sample size

cat("Max R-squared shrinkage (apparent - adjusted): 0.05\n")

  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = min_n,
      unit = "participants_total"
    )

  simulation = NULL
)

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the

          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

answer.summary: Using pmsampsize version 1.1.3 with Riley et al. (2018, 2020) binary outcome prediction model development criteria, the minimum total sample size required is **1482 participants**. This calculation incorporates 10 candidate predictor parameters, outcome prevalence of 0.20, anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared of 0.12, and anticipated shrinkage of 0.95. The binding constraint is Criterion 1 (overfitting control via shrinkage ≥ 0.90), which requires N = 1482. At this sample size, the expected margin of error for average outcome-risk estimation is 0.0204 (95% CI), which comfortably satisfies the target of ≤0.05.
answer.method: Riley binary outcome prediction model development sample size calculation (pmsampsize 1.1.3)
assumptions: Binary logistic regression model development cohort design with no external validation in this calculation
Anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared of 0.12 reflects the target predictive performance baseline
Anticipated shrinkage of 0.95 reflects expected loss due to overfitting (5% overfitting = 10% allowable shrinkage)
pmsampsize default absolute precision criteria: maximum 0.05 difference between apparent and adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared; target margin of error ≤0.05 at 95% CI for average predicted risk
95% confidence interval construction for margin of error calculation
Outcome prevalence 0.20 is constant across development and validation populations
Model will use 10 candidate predictors with typical parametrization (each predictor requires one parameter estimate)
limitations: Calculation assumes the anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared of 0.12 is reasonable and achievable with the 10 candidate predictors; actual model performance may differ
Shrinkage assumption of 0.95 is optimistic (5% overfitting) and assumes careful model development practices; higher overfitting may occur in practice
Sample size does not include provision for missing data, study dropout, or attrition—these should be added separately if applicable
Margin of error formula assumes simple random sampling; complex survey designs or clustering would require adjustment
Calculation is based on marginal (overall) prevalence; differential prevalence by subgroups not considered

# Install and load pmsampsize for Riley binary development criteria
# Verify version 1.1.3 is available
if (!require("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize")
}
library(pmsampsize)

# Check package version
cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(packageVersion("pmsampsize")), "\n\n")

# Set parameters according to user specification
p <- 10              # number of candidate predictor parameters
prevalence <- 0.20   # outcome prevalence (20%)
r.sq <- 0.12         # anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
shrinkage <- 0.95    # anticipated shrinkage factor
margin.error <- 0.05 # target average outcome-risk absolute margin of error
conf.level <- 0.95   # confidence level (95%)
overfitting.max <- 0.05  # max absolute apparent-adjusted R-squared difference (Nagelkerke)

# Use pmsampsize for binary outcome prediction model development
# The function calculates sample size for two precision criteria:
# 1. Limiting overfitting (apparent vs adjusted R-squared difference)
# 2. Average outcome-risk precision

result <- pmsampsize(type = "b",  # binary outcome
                     p = p,        # number of candidate parameters
                     prevcase = prevalence,  # outcome prevalence
                     r.sq = r.sq,  # anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
                     shrinkage = shrinkage,  # anticipated shrinkage factor
                     margin.error = margin.error  # absolute margin of error for average predicted risk
)

# Display the results
cat("="*70, "\n")
cat("RILEY BINARY MODEL DEVELOPMENT SAMPLE SIZE CALCULATION\n")
cat("="*70, "\n\n")

print(result)

# Extract the sample size
minimum_n <- result$Minimum_sample_size

cat("\n", "="*70, "\n")
cat("MINIMUM SAMPLE SIZE REQUIRED:", minimum_n, "participants (total)\n")
cat("="*70, "\n\n")

# Verify the precision at the returned sample size
cat("VERIFICATION OF PRECISION AT RETURNED SAMPLE SIZE (n =", minimum_n, ")\n")
cat("-"*70, "\n\n")

# Extract additional information from the result object
cat("Anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared:", r.sq, "\n")
cat("Anticipated shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Expected adjusted R-squared in validation:", r.sq * shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Number of predictor parameters:", p, "\n")
cat("Outcome prevalence:", prevalence, "\n")
cat("Confidence level:", conf.level, "\n")
cat("Target margin of error (absolute):", margin.error, "\n\n")

# Display result summary
cat("Result object contents:\n")
str(result)

# Create JSON output
results_list <- list(
  metric = "sample_size",
  value = minimum_n,
  unit = "participants_total"
)

cat("\n\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(list(results = list(results_list)), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))
