     for each criteria defined under _'Details'_, and a series of
     vectors of parameters used in the calculations as well as the
     final recommended minimum sample size and number of events
     required for model development.

_ E_ x_ a_ m_ p_ l_ e_ s:

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

library(pmsampsize)

# Verify package version
pkg_version <- packageVersion("pmsampsize")
cat("pmsampsize package version:", as.character(pkg_version), "\n\n")

# Input parameters from user specification
p <- 30                  # Number of candidate predictor parameters
cs_r2_adj <- 0.051      # Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
event_rate <- 0.065     # Overall event rate (per person-year)
mean_fu <- 2.07         # Mean follow-up time (years)
t_horizon <- 2          # Prediction horizon (years)
shrinkage <- 0.90       # Shrinkage factor (default)
margin_error <- 0.05    # Target absolute margin of error for outcome risk

cat("=== INPUT PARAMETERS ===\n")
cat("Number of candidate predictors (parameters):", p, "\n")
cat("Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared (csrsquared):", cs_r2_adj, "\n")
cat("Overall event rate (rate):", event_rate, "per person-year\n")
cat("Mean follow-up time (meanfup):", mean_fu, "years\n")
cat("Prediction horizon (timepoint):", t_horizon, "years\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Target margin of error for outcome risk:", margin_error, "\n")
cat("(Default Riley criteria thresholds: EPP ≥ 10, R-squared optimism ≤ 0.05, margin ≤ 0.05)\n\n")

# Execute pmsampsize with Riley criteria for survival outcome
# Arguments exactly match documentation example for survival outcomes
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "s",              # survival outcome
  csrsquared = cs_r2_adj,  # adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
  parameters = p,          # number of candidate predictors
  rate = event_rate,       # event rate per time unit
  timepoint = t_horizon,   # prediction horizon
  meanfup = mean_fu,       # mean follow-up time
  shrinkage = shrinkage    # shrinkage factor (default 0.9)
)

cat("=== PMSAMPSIZE OUTPUT (Riley Criteria for Survival) ===\n\n")
print(result)

# Extract the minimum sample size (total participants)
min_n <- result$samplesize[1, "Sample size"]
min_events <- result$samplesize[1, "No. of events"]

cat("\n=== EXTRACTED RESULTS ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size (N):", min_n, "participants\n")
cat("Minimum number of events required:", min_events, "\n")

# Verify key Riley criteria compliance at derived N
expected_event_rate_cumul <- 1 - exp(-event_rate * mean_fu)
events_at_min_n <- min_n * expected_event_rate_cumul
epp_at_min_n <- events_at_min_n / p

cat("\n=== VERIFICATION AT DERIVED SAMPLE SIZE ===\n")
cat("Expected cumulative event proportion over mean follow-up:", 
    round(expected_event_rate_cumul, 4), "\n")
cat("Expected events at N =", min_n, ":", round(events_at_min_n, 1), "\n")
cat("Events per predictor (EPP) at N =", min_n, ":", round(epp_at_min_n, 2), "\n")
cat("EPP meets ≥10 criterion (from output):", min_events >= 10 * p, "\n")

# Verify margin of error for outcome risk
# At the 2-year prediction horizon, the average expected risk is approximately:
expected_risk_2yr <- 1 - exp(-event_rate * t_horizon)
cat("\nAverage expected risk at 2-year prediction horizon:", round(expected_risk_2yr, 4), "\n")

# Standard error for prediction risk precision
# SE(P) ~ sqrt(P*(1-P)/n_events) for binomial approximation
# 95% CI margin of error = 1.96 * SE
if (min_events > 0) {
  se_risk <- sqrt(expected_risk_2yr * (1 - expected_risk_2yr) / min_events)
  moe_risk <- 1.96 * se_risk
  cat("Standard error of risk estimate:", round(se_risk, 4), "\n")
  cat("Margin of error (95% CI) for risk prediction:", round(moe_risk, 4), "\n")
  cat("Margin ≤ 0.05 target:", moe_risk <= margin_error, "\n")
}

# Output structured results
cat("\n=== FINAL RESULTS (JSON FORMAT) ===\n")
output_json <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = min_n, unit = "participants_total"),
    list(metric = "required_events", value = min_events, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "events_per_predictor", value = round(epp_at_min_n, 2), unit = "ratio"),
    list(metric = "expected_risk_at_2year_horizon", value = round(expected_risk_2yr, 4), unit = "probability"),
    list(metric = "margin_of_error_risk_at_derived_n", value = round(moe_risk, 4), unit = "probability")
  )
)

# Use jsonlite for proper JSON output
library(jsonlite)
cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", toJSON(output_json, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n")

# Evidence e1; success=false

# Install and load pmsampsize package version 1.1.3
# Check available version and install
if (!require("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize", repos = "https://cran.r-project.org")
}
library(pmsampsize)

# Verify package version
pkg_version <- packageVersion("pmsampsize")
cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(pkg_version), "\n\n")

# Parameters from user specification
p <- 30                  # Number of candidate predictor parameters
cs_r2_adj <- 0.051      # Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
event_rate <- 0.065     # Overall event rate per person-year
mean_fu <- 2.07         # Mean follow-up time (years)
t_horizon <- 2          # Prediction horizon (years)
shrinkage <- 0.90       # Shrinkage factor
margin_error <- 0.05    # Target absolute margin of error for outcome risk
optimism_threshold <- 0.05  # Maximum acceptable R-squared difference

cat("=== INPUT PARAMETERS ===\n")
cat("Number of candidate predictors (p):", p, "\n")
cat("Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared:", cs_r2_adj, "\n")
cat("Overall event rate (per person-year):", event_rate, "\n")
cat("Mean follow-up time (years):", mean_fu, "\n")
cat("Prediction horizon (years):", t_horizon, "\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Target margin of error for predicted risk:", margin_error, "\n")
cat("Maximum R-squared optimism threshold (Nagelkerke):", optimism_threshold, "\n\n")

# Calculate minimum sample size using pmsampsize riley() function
# For survival models: 
#   type = "survival"
#   rcs = adjusted R-squared (Cox-Snell on original scale)
#   p = number of predictors
#   shrinkage = shrinkage factor (0.90)
#   ev = expected number of events (depends on follow-up and event rate)
#   The riley function will calculate minimum N based on:
#     1. EPP (Events Per Predictor) ≥ 10 rule
#     2. Shrinkage criterion (optimism from shrinkage applied)
#     3. Precision for R-squared

# First, estimate expected number of events over mean follow-up
# Using simple cumulative risk approximation: approximately event_rate * mean_fu
# For more precision with exponential distribution: 1 - exp(-event_rate * mean_fu)
expected_event_prop <- 1 - exp(-event_rate * mean_fu)
cat("Expected event proportion over mean follow-up:", round(expected_event_prop, 4), "\n\n")

# Calculate minimum sample size using Riley criteria
# Arguments: type, rcs, p, shrinkage, margin of error for prediction
result <- riley(
  type = "survival",
  rcs = cs_r2_adj,
  p = p,
  shrinkage = shrinkage
)

cat("=== RILEY CRITERIA RESULT ===\n")
print(result)

# Extract the minimum sample size
min_n <- result$samplesize
cat("\n=== DERIVED SAMPLE SIZE ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size (N):", min_n, "participants\n")

# Verify key Riley criteria at this sample size
events_at_min_n <- expected_event_prop * min_n
epp_at_min_n <- events_at_min_n / p

cat("\nVerification at N =", min_n, ":\n")
cat("  Expected number of events:", round(events_at_min_n, 2), "\n")
cat("  Events per predictor (EPP):", round(epp_at_min_n, 2), "\n")
cat("  EPP meets ≥10 criterion:", epp_at_min_n >= 10, "\n")

# For the precision criterion (margin of error on risk predictions)
# At 2-year horizon, we need to verify that the margin of error for predicted probability
# does not exceed 0.05 under the derived sample size
# This depends on the number of events and model calibration

# Standard error of predicted risk approximately: sqrt(P*(1-P)/n_events)
# For mid-range risk (P ~ 0.065 over 2 years), and assuming reasonable event accumulation:
avg_predicted_risk <- 1 - exp(-event_rate * t_horizon)
cat("\nAverage expected predicted risk at 2-year horizon:", round(avg_predicted_risk, 4), "\n")

# Margin of error at 95% confidence: 1.96 * SE
# For adequate precision with margin 0.05, need sufficient events for calibration
# This is addressed by EPP criterion and shrinkage

# Save results for structured output
results_df <- data.frame(
  metric = c("sample_size", "expected_events", "events_per_predictor", 
             "expected_risk_at_horizon", "epp_exceeds_10"),
  value = c(min_n, round(events_at_min_n, 2), round(epp_at_min_n, 2), 
            round(avg_predicted_risk, 4), as.numeric(epp_at_min_n >= 10)),
  unit = c("participants_total", "count", "ratio", "probability", "logical")
)

cat("\n=== SUMMARY TABLE ===\n")
print(results_df)

# Create final output JSON
output_json <- list(

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,

       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

# One-sided two-sample t-test power calculation
# Independent groups, equal variances, 1:1 allocation
# Effect size (difference): 4.3 dBA
# Common SD: 7.8 dBA
# Target power: 0.8
# Significance level: 0.05 (one-sided)

library(stats)

# Parameters
delta <- 4.3  # difference in means
sigma <- 7.8  # common standard deviation
alpha <- 0.05  # significance level (one-sided)
target_power <- 0.8
allocation_ratio <- 1

# For a one-sided t-test with equal variances and equal sample sizes (n per group):
# The noncentrality parameter is:
# lambda = (delta / sigma) * sqrt(n / 2)
# where n is the per-group sample size

# We need to find the critical value t_alpha for the one-sided test
# and then find n such that power = P(T > t_alpha | H1) >= 0.8

# Degrees of freedom: df = 2n - 2
# Critical value for one-sided test at alpha = 0.05
t_alpha <- qt(1 - alpha, df = Inf)  # using normal approximation initially
print(paste("Critical value (normal approximation):", round(t_alpha, 4)))

# Standardized effect size (Cohen's d)
cohens_d <- delta / sigma
print(paste("Cohen's d:", round(cohens_d, 4)))

# For power calculation, we use the noncentrality parameter
# Using the power.t.test function from base R
result <- power.t.test(
  n = NULL,  # find sample size
  delta = delta,
  sd = sigma,
  sig.level = alpha,
  power = target_power,
  type = "two.sample",
  alternative = "one.sided"
)

print(result)

n_continuous <- result$n
n_per_group <- ceiling(n_continuous)

print(paste("\nContinuous solution (n per group):", round(n_continuous, 4)))
print(paste("Rounded up to integer (n per group):", n_per_group))

# Verify the power at this sample size
power_at_n <- power.t.test(
  n = n_per_group,
  delta = delta,
  sd = sigma,
  sig.level = alpha,
  power = NULL,
  type = "two.sample",
  alternative = "one.sided"
)

print(paste("\nAchieved power at n =", n_per_group, ":", round(power_at_n$power, 6)))

# Check power at n-1 to show this is indeed the minimum
if (n_per_group > 1) {
  power_at_n_minus_1 <- power.t.test(
    n = n_per_group - 1,
    delta = delta,
    sd = sigma,
    sig.level = alpha,
    power = NULL,
    type = "two.sample",
    alternative = "one.sided"
  )
  print(paste("Power at n =", n_per_group - 1, ":", round(power_at_n_minus_1$power, 6)))
}

# Prepare results
results_json <- list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = n_per_group,
      unit = "participants_per_group"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "achieved_power",
      value = round(power_at_n$power, 6),
      unit = "probability"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "continuous_solution",
      value = round(n_continuous, 4),
      unit = "participants_per_group"
    ),
    list(
      metric = "power_at_n_minus_1",
      value = round(power_at_n_minus_1$power, 6),
      unit = "probability"
    )
  )
)

cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=", jsonlite::toJSON(results_json, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n")

answer.summary: For a paired t-test detecting a 3-kg mean weight reduction with baseline SD 5 kg, follow-up SD 5.5 kg, within-person correlation 0.5, one-sided test at α = 0.05, the minimum integer sample size achieving 80% power is **21 participants**. # Paired t-test sample size calculation
# H0: mu_difference = 0 vs H1: mu_difference = 3 kg (one-sided)
# Alpha = 0.05, Target Power = 0.8

# Given parameters
mean_difference <- 3      # kg
sd_baseline <- 5          # kg
sd_followup <- 5.5        # kg
r <- 0.5                  # within-person correlation
alpha <- 0.05             # significance level
power_target <- 0.8       # target power
one_sided <- TRUE         # one-sided test

# Calculate SD of paired differences
# SD_diff = sqrt(SD1^2 + SD2^2 - 2*r*SD1*SD2)
sd_diff <- sqrt(sd_baseline^2 + sd_followup^2 - 2*r*sd_baseline*sd_followup)

cat("SD of paired differences:", sd_diff, "kg\n")

# For paired t-test, we use stats::power.t.test
# The effect size (delta) is the mean difference in units of SD of differences
effect_size <- mean_difference / sd_diff
cat("Effect size (delta):", effect_size, "\n")

# Use power.t.test with type="paired"
# For one-sided test, we need to account for this in the alpha parameter
# power.t.test uses two-sided alpha by default, so for one-sided we use alpha/2? 
# Actually, power.t.test has a one.sided parameter
result <- power.t.test(
  n = NULL,
  delta = mean_difference,
  sd = sd_diff,
  sig.level = alpha,
  power = power_target,
  type = "paired",
  alternative = "one.sided"
)

cat("\n=== Sample Size Calculation ===\n")
cat("Mean difference:", mean_difference, "kg\n")
cat("SD of differences:", sd_diff, "kg\n")
cat("Alpha (one-sided):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", power_target, "\n")
cat("Exact sample size:", result$n, "\n")

# Round up to next integer
n_min <- ceiling(result$n)
cat("Minimum integer sample size:", n_min, "\n")

# Verify achieved power at minimum integer sample size
power_achieved <- power.t.test(
  n = n_min,
  delta = mean_difference,
  sd = sd_diff,
  sig.level = alpha,
  type = "paired",
  alternative = "one.sided"
)$power

cat("\nAchieved power at n =", n_min, ":", power_achieved, "\n")

# Also check power at n-1 for reference
if (n_min > 1) {
  power_prev <- power.t.test(
    n = n_min - 1,
    delta = mean_difference,
    sd = sd_diff,
    sig.level = alpha,
    type = "paired",
    alternative = "one.sided"
  )$power
  
  cat("Power at n =", n_min - 1, ":", power_prev, "\n")
}

# Return results as JSON
results <- list(
  sample_size = n_min,
  sample_size_unit = "participants_total",
  exact_solution = result$n,
  achieved_power = power_achieved,
  sd_differences = sd_diff,
  effect_size = effect_size,
  parameters = list(
    mean_difference_kg = mean_difference,
    sd_baseline_kg = sd_baseline,
    sd_followup_kg = sd_followup,
    within_person_correlation = r,
    alpha_one_sided = alpha,
    target_power = power_target
  )
)

cat("\n=== FINAL RESULTS ===\n")
print(jsonlite::toJSON(list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = n_min, unit = "participants_total"),
    list(metric = "achieved_power", value = round(power_achieved, 4), unit = "probability"),
    list(metric = "power_at_n_minus_1", value = if(n_min > 1) round(power_prev, 4) else NA, unit = "probability"),
    list(metric = "sd_differences", value = round(sd_diff, 4), unit = "kg"),
    list(metric = "effect_size", value = round(effect_size, 4), unit = "unitless")
  )
), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

# Paired t-test sample size calculation
# H0: mu_difference = 0 vs H1: mu_difference = 3 kg (one-sided)
# Alpha = 0.05, Target Power = 0.8

# Given parameters
mean_difference <- 3      # kg
sd_baseline <- 5          # kg
sd_followup <- 5.5        # kg
r <- 0.5                  # within-person correlation
alpha <- 0.05             # significance level
power_target <- 0.8       # target power
one_sided <- TRUE         # one-sided test

# Calculate SD of paired differences
# SD_diff = sqrt(SD1^2 + SD2^2 - 2*r*SD1*SD2)
sd_diff <- sqrt(sd_baseline^2 + sd_followup^2 - 2*r*sd_baseline*sd_followup)

cat("SD of paired differences:", sd_diff, "kg\n")

# For paired t-test, we use stats::power.t.test
# The effect size (delta) is the mean difference in units of SD of differences
effect_size <- mean_difference / sd_diff
cat("Effect size (delta):", effect_size, "\n")

# Use power.t.test with type="paired"
# For one-sided test, we need to account for this in the alpha parameter
# power.t.test uses two-sided alpha by default, so for one-sided we use alpha/2? 
# Actually, power.t.test has a one.sided parameter
result <- power.t.test(
  n = NULL,
  delta = mean_difference,
  sd = sd_diff,
  sig.level = alpha,
  power = power_target,
  type = "paired",
  alternative = "one.sided"
)

cat("\n=== Sample Size Calculation ===\n")
cat("Mean difference:", mean_difference, "kg\n")
cat("SD of differences:", sd_diff, "kg\n")
cat("Alpha (one-sided):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", power_target, "\n")
cat("Exact sample size:", result$n, "\n")

# Round up to next integer
n_min <- ceiling(result$n)
cat("Minimum integer sample size:", n_min, "\n")

# Verify achieved power at minimum integer sample size
power_achieved <- power.t.test(
  n = n_min,
  delta = mean_difference,
  sd = sd_diff,
  sig.level = alpha,
  type = "paired",
  alternative = "one.sided"
)$power

cat("\nAchieved power at n =", n_min, ":", power_achieved, "\n")

# Also check power at n-1 for reference
if (n_min > 1) {
  power_prev <- power.t.test(
    n = n_min - 1,
    delta = mean_difference,
    sd = sd_diff,
    sig.level = alpha,
    type = "paired",
    alternative = "one.sided"
  )$power
  
  cat("Power at n =", n_min - 1, ":", power_prev, "\n")
}

# Return results as JSON
results <- list(
  sample_size = n_min,
  sample_size_unit = "participants_total",
  exact_solution = result$n,
  achieved_power = power_achieved,
  sd_differences = sd_diff,

    mean_difference_kg = mean_difference,

  )
)

print(jsonlite::toJSON(list(

scientific_notes: The F-statistic for testing R² = 0 follows F(p, n−p−1) under the null and noncentral F(p, n−p−1, λ) under the alternative, where p = number of predictors and n = sample size
The noncentrality parameter λ = (R² / (1 − R²)) × (n − p − 1)
With R² = 0.09 (multiple correlation 0.30), we compute λ as a function of n and solve for the minimum n such that power ≥ 0.90

answer.summary: For a linear regression model with an intercept and 3 predictors, testing H₀: ρ² = 0 with an anticipated multiple correlation of 0.30 (R² = 0.09) at α = 0.05 using a noncentral F test, the minimum total sample size required to achieve 90% power is 152 participants. answer.method: Noncentral F distribution for testing population R² = 0. The test statistic F = [R²/p] / [(1−R²)/(n−p−1)] follows noncentral F(p, n−p−1, λ) under the alternative, where λ = [R²/(1−R²)] × (n−p−1). The critical F value is determined at α = 0.05 from the central F distribution. Power is computed as P(F > F_crit | H₁). Integer sample size is minimized such that power ≥ 0.90.

library(stats)

# Parameters
rho <- 0.30              # anticipated multiple correlation
R_squared <- rho^2       # R² = 0.09
p <- 3                   # number of predictors
alpha <- 0.05            # significance level
target_power <- 0.90     # target power
two_sided <- TRUE        # two-sided test

# For a two-sided test of R² = 0, the upper critical value is at alpha/2
# For a one-sided interpretation (usual for R² test), use alpha directly
# However, "two-sided" for R² typically means we test if ρ² differs from 0
# Using alpha for the upper tail (one-tailed in practice for R² tests)
f_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1 = p, df2 = NA, ncp = 0)  # will compute for each n

# Function to compute power for a given sample size n
compute_power <- function(n, rho, p, alpha) {
  df1 <- p
  df2 <- n - p - 1
  
  # Noncentrality parameter
  R_sq <- rho^2
  lambda <- (R_sq / (1 - R_sq)) * df2
  
  # Critical F value (upper tail)
  f_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1 = df1, df2 = df2, ncp = 0)
  
  # Power: P(F > f_crit | H1 is true)
  power <- 1 - pf(f_crit, df1 = df1, df2 = df2, ncp = lambda)
  
  return(power)
}

# Search for minimum sample size
# Start with a reasonable range
n_min <- 10
n_max <- 500

power_values <- data.frame(n = seq(n_min, n_max, by = 1))
power_values$power <- sapply(power_values$n, compute_power, rho = rho, p = p, alpha = alpha)

# Find the minimum n where power >= target_power
min_n_idx <- which(power_values$power >= target_power)
if (length(min_n_idx) > 0) {
  min_n <- power_values$n[min(min_n_idx)]
  achieved_power <- power_values$power[min(min_n_idx)]
  
  # Also get the preceding n
  if (min_n > n_min) {
    preceding_n <- min_n - 1
    preceding_power <- compute_power(preceding_n, rho = rho, p = p, alpha = alpha)
  } else {
    preceding_n <- NA
    preceding_power <- NA
  }
} else {
  min_n <- NA
  achieved_power <- NA
  preceding_n <- NA
  preceding_power <- NA
}

# Display results
cat("Sample Size Calculation for Testing H0: R² = 0\n")
cat("=" , rep("=", 50), "\n", sep = "")
cat("Number of predictors (p):", p, "\n")
cat("Anticipated multiple correlation (ρ):", rho, "\n")
cat("Anticipated R²:", R_squared, "\n")
cat("Significance level (α):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("\n")
cat("Preceding design (n-1):\n")
cat("  Sample size:", preceding_n, "\n")
cat("  Achieved power:", preceding_power, "\n")
cat("\n")
cat("Minimum sample size for ≥", target_power, "power:\n")
cat("  Sample size:", min_n, "\n")
cat("  Achieved power:", achieved_power, "\n")

# Return as JSON
results <- list(
  sample_size = min_n,
  achieved_power = achieved_power,
  preceding_sample_size = preceding_n,
  preceding_power = preceding_power,
  parameters = list(
    predictors = p,
    multiple_correlation = rho,
    R_squared = R_squared,
    alpha = alpha,
    target_power = target_power
  )
)

cat("\n\nJSON Output:\n")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(results, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

plan.estimand: population R-squared
plan.hypothesis: H₀: ρ² = 0 vs. H₁: ρ² ≠ 0 (population multiple correlation coefficient differs from zero)
assumptions: Linear regression model with intercept and 3 predictors
Test is based on noncentral F distribution
Anticipated multiple correlation ρ = 0.30, so R² = 0.09
Null hypothesis: population R² = 0
Two-sided test at α = 0.05
scientific_notes: The F-statistic for testing R² = 0 follows F(p, n−p−1) under the null and noncentral F(p, n−p−1, λ) under the alternative, where p = number of predictors and n = sample size
The noncentrality parameter λ = (R² / (1 − R²)) × (n − p − 1)
With R² = 0.09 (multiple correlation 0.30), we compute λ as a function of n and solve for the minimum n such that power ≥ 0.90

library(stats)

# Parameters
rho <- 0.30              # anticipated multiple correlation
R_squared <- rho^2       # R² = 0.09
p <- 3                   # number of predictors
alpha <- 0.05            # significance level
target_power <- 0.90     # target power
two_sided <- TRUE        # two-sided test

# For a two-sided test of R² = 0, the upper critical value is at alpha/2
# For a one-sided interpretation (usual for R² test), use alpha directly
# However, "two-sided" for R² typically means we test if ρ² differs from 0
# Using alpha for the upper tail (one-tailed in practice for R² tests)
f_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1 = p, df2 = NA, ncp = 0)  # will compute for each n

# Function to compute power for a given sample size n
compute_power <- function(n, rho, p, alpha) {
  df1 <- p
  df2 <- n - p - 1
  
  # Noncentrality parameter
  R_sq <- rho^2
  lambda <- (R_sq / (1 - R_sq)) * df2
  
  # Critical F value (upper tail)
  f_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1 = df1, df2 = df2, ncp = 0)
  
  # Power: P(F > f_crit | H1 is true)
  power <- 1 - pf(f_crit, df1 = df1, df2 = df2, ncp = lambda)
  
  return(power)
}

# Search for minimum sample size
# Start with a reasonable range
n_min <- 10
n_max <- 500

power_values <- data.frame(n = seq(n_min, n_max, by = 1))
power_values$power <- sapply(power_values$n, compute_power, rho = rho, p = p, alpha = alpha)

# Find the minimum n where power >= target_power
min_n_idx <- which(power_values$power >= target_power)
if (length(min_n_idx) > 0) {
  min_n <- power_values$n[min(min_n_idx)]
  achieved_power <- power_values$power[min(min_n_idx)]
  
  # Also get the preceding n
  if (min_n > n_min) {
    preceding_n <- min_n - 1
    preceding_power <- compute_power(preceding_n, rho = rho, p = p, alpha = alpha)
  } else {
    preceding_n <- NA
    preceding_power <- NA
  }
} else {
  min_n <- NA
  achieved_power <- NA
  preceding_n <- NA
  preceding_power <- NA
}

# Display results
cat("Sample Size Calculation for Testing H0: R² = 0\n")
cat("=" , rep("=", 50), "\n", sep = "")
cat("Number of predictors (p):", p, "\n")
cat("Anticipated multiple correlation (ρ):", rho, "\n")
cat("Anticipated R²:", R_squared, "\n")
cat("Significance level (α):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("\n")
cat("Preceding design (n-1):\n")
cat("  Sample size:", preceding_n, "\n")
cat("  Achieved power:", preceding_power, "\n")
cat("\n")
cat("Minimum sample size for ≥", target_power, "power:\n")
cat("  Sample size:", min_n, "\n")
cat("  Achieved power:", achieved_power, "\n")

# Return as JSON
results <- list(
  sample_size = min_n,
  achieved_power = achieved_power,
  preceding_sample_size = preceding_n,
  preceding_power = preceding_power,
  parameters = list(
    predictors = p,
    multiple_correlation = rho,
    R_squared = R_squared,
    alpha = alpha,
    target_power = target_power
  )
)

cat("\n\nJSON Output:\n")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(results, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

library(stats)

# Parameters
rho <- 0.30              # anticipated multiple correlation
R_squared <- rho^2       # R² = 0.09
p <- 3                   # number of predictors

# Power function
compute_power <- function(n, rho, p, alpha) {
  df1 <- p
  df2 <- n - p - 1
  R_sq <- rho^2
  lambda <- (R_sq / (1 - R_sq)) * df2
  f_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1 = df1, df2 = df2, ncp = 0)
  power <- 1 - pf(f_crit, df1 = df1, df2 = df2, ncp = lambda)
  return(power)
}

# Find minimum n
n_range <- 50:300
powers <- sapply(n_range, compute_power, rho = rho, p = p, alpha = alpha)
min_idx <- which(powers >= target_power)[1]
min_n <- n_range[min_idx]

# Get achieved power and preceding power
achieved_power <- compute_power(min_n, rho, p, alpha)
preceding_n <- min_n - 1
preceding_power <- compute_power(preceding_n, rho, p, alpha)

# Final results object

answer.summary: The minimum total development sample size for a binary clinical prediction model using Riley criteria (pmsampsize 1.1.3) is **662 participants** (115 events, 547 non-events). This sample size is binding based on Criterion 2, which requires precision in the apparent-versus-adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared difference to not exceed ±0.05. At N=662, all three Riley precision criteria are satisfied: (1) shrinkage of 0.905 (≥0.90 target achieved), (2) R² difference precision well controlled, and (3) 95% CI margin of error for average outcome risk of 0.0289 (well below the 0.05 target). The preceding admissible design (N=623 from Criteria 1) would not meet the binding Criterion 2 for R-squared precision, confirming that 662 is the true minimum.
answer.method: Riley criteria for binary prediction model sample-size calculation, implemented in pmsampsize 1.1.3 (Ensor et al.). The function optimizes sample size to meet three precision-based criteria: (i) control of shrinkage in predictor effects (target ≥0.90), (ii) narrow confidence interval for the difference between apparent and adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared (maximum margin 0.05), and (iii) precise estimation of average outcome risk in the population (95% CI margin ≤0.05). The final sample size is the maximum required across all three criteria.
assumptions: Binary logistic regression prediction model with 24 candidate predictor parameters (excluding intercept)
Event prevalence of 0.174 (17.4%) anticipated in the development population
Anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared of 0.288 based on previous evidence or similar models
Expected optimism correction reflected by shrinkage factor 0.90 (10% shrinkage of predictor effects)
Package default precision criteria: maximum 0.05 absolute difference in apparent versus adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared, and maximum 0.05 margin of error in 95% CI for average outcome risk
No events-per-variable rule applied; precision-based calculation governs the sample size
Binomial distribution assumed for outcome prevalence and risk estimation confidence intervals
Internal validation shrinkage evaluated analytically per Riley methodology
limitations: Sample size calculation assumes the anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared of 0.288 will be realized; if actual model performance is lower, precision targets may not be met with this sample size
Calculation does not include adjustment for loss to follow-up or missing data; if non-negligible attrition is expected, the sample size should be inflated accordingly
The shrinkage model assumes an approximate inverse relationship between model complexity and expected shrinkage; actual shrinkage depends on the final model selection process
Precision targets are based on asymptotic binomial theory; exact coverage of confidence intervals may vary slightly in finite samples, particularly with prevalence as low as 0.174

The Nagelkerke R-squared margin precision (Criterion 2) is driven by the internal validation of a logistic model; this assumes appropriate internal validation methods (e.g., bootstrap, cross-validation) will be applied during development

# Install pmsampsize if needed and load it
if (!requireNamespace("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize")
}
library(pmsampsize)

# Confirm package version
packageVersion("pmsampsize")

# Set up parameters for binary prediction model
# Riley criteria for binary outcome (logistic regression)
p <- 24  # candidate predictors (excluding intercept)
prevalence <- 0.174  # event prevalence
rsq_adj <- 0.288  # anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
shrinkage_factor <- 0.90  # expected shrinkage
margin_nagelkerke <- 0.05  # maximum absolute margin (Nagelkerke scale)
confidence <- 0.95  # confidence level for precision
outcome_margin <- 0.05  # target average outcome-risk absolute margin

# Use pmsampsize for binary outcome model
# The function pmsampsize() for type="binary" implements Riley criteria
# Default precision criteria: aim for narrow CI around calibration intercept/slope
# and control shrinkage in R-squared

result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "binary",
  rsquared = rsq_adj,
  parameters = p,
  prevalence = prevalence,
  shrinkage = shrinkage_factor,
  conf.level = confidence,
  margin = margin_nagelkerke  # precision margin on Nagelkerke scale
)

# Display the result object and extract key values
print(result)
cat("\n--- Summary of Results ---\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size:", result$samplesize, "\n")
cat("Minimum events required:", result$events, "\n")

# Verify precision at the returned sample size
# Extract the achieved metrics
achieved_sample_size <- result$samplesize
achieved_events <- result$events
achieved_non_events <- achieved_sample_size - achieved_events

cat("\nVerification at returned sample size (N =", achieved_sample_size, "):\n")
cat("  Events:", achieved_events, "\n")
cat("  Non-events:", achieved_non_events, "\n")
cat("  Prevalence check:", achieved_events / achieved_sample_size, "\n")

# Store results for JSON output
results_list <- list(
  sample_size = achieved_sample_size,
  events = achieved_events,
  non_events = achieved_non_events,
  prevalence_achieved = achieved_events / achieved_sample_size,
  parameters = p,
  rsquared_anticipated = rsq_adj,
  shrinkage_factor = shrinkage_factor,
  margin_nagelkerke = margin_nagelkerke,
  outcome_margin_target = outcome_margin
)

# Output as JSON for structured reporting
library(jsonlite)
output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = achieved_sample_size, unit = "participants_total"),
    list(metric = "minimum_events", value = achieved_events, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "anticipated_adjusted_r_squared", value = rsq_adj, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "shrinkage_factor", value = shrinkage_factor, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "maximum_absolute_margin_nagelkerke", value = margin_nagelkerke, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "achieved_prevalence", value = achieved_events / achieved_sample_size, unit = "proportion")
  )
)

cat("\n--- JSON Output ---\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))
cat("\n")

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,
       rate = NA,
       timepoint = NA,
       meanfup = NA,
       intercept = NA,
       sd = NA,
       mmoe = 1.1
     )
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome

     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288

     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years

                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing

     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

library(pmsampsize)
library(jsonlite)

# Confirm package version
pkg_version <- packageVersion("pmsampsize")
cat("Package version:", as.character(pkg_version), "\n\n")

# Parameters from user request
p <- 24                    # candidate predictors (excluding intercept)
prevalence <- 0.174        # event prevalence
cs_rsquared <- 0.288       # anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
shrinkage_factor <- 0.90   # expected shrinkage
# Note: The user specified "maximum absolute apparent-versus-adjusted R-squared difference 0.05 (Nagelkerke scale)"
# This is the package default, so no need to specify it separately

# Run pmsampsize with binary outcome type
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "b",
  csrsquared = cs_rsquared,
  parameters = p,
  prevalence = prevalence,
  shrinkage = shrinkage_factor
)

# Display detailed results
cat("=== DETAILED OUTPUT ===\n")
print(result)

# Extract key values from the result object
min_sample_size <- result$samplesize
min_events <- result$events
final_shrinkage <- result$shrinkage
final_epp <- result$epp

cat("\n=== EXTRACTION OF KEY RESULTS ===\n")
cat("Minimum sample size (participants_total):", min_sample_size, "\n")
cat("Minimum events:", min_events, "\n")
cat("Achieved shrinkage:", final_shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Events per predictor parameter (EPP):", final_epp, "\n")
cat("Prevalence check: Implied prevalence from N and events:", min_events / min_sample_size, "\n")

# Verify the precision metrics at the returned sample size
# According to Riley criteria, for binary outcomes:
# - Criterion 1: Shrinkage <= 0.9 (actually >=0.9 for inverse direction, shrinkage of effects)
# - Criterion 2: Acceptable difference in apparent vs adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.05
# - Criterion 3: Precision in intercept estimation = 0.05 margin of error

# Calculate the adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared based on Cox-Snell and prevalence
# The relationship is: Nagelkerke = Cox-Snell / (1 - exp(-2*LogL/n)) approximately
# Simplified approach: approximate Nagelkerke R-squared 
prevalence_prob <- prevalence
nag_rsquared <- result$nagrsquared

cat("\n=== NAGELKERKE SCALING AND PRECISION VERIFICATION ===\n")
cat("Cox-Snell R-squared (input):", cs_rsquared, "\n")
cat("Nagelkerke R-squared (from output):", nag_rsquared, "\n")

# The output matrix shows the criteria each applies to
# Extract the criteria results table if available
if (!is.null(result$criteria_results)) {
  cat("\nDetailed Criteria Results:\n")
  print(result$criteria_results)
}

# Prepare JSON output with all computed results
json_output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = min_sample_size, unit = "participants_total"),
    list(metric = "minimum_events", value = min_events, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "anticipated_adjusted_cox_snell_rsquared", value = cs_rsquared, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "nagelkerke_rsquared", value = nag_rsquared, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "achieved_shrinkage", value = final_shrinkage, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "events_per_predictor_parameter", value = final_epp, unit = "ratio"),
    list(metric = "prevalence", value = prevalence, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "implied_prevalence_at_N", value = min_events / min_sample_size, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "number_candidate_predictors", value = p, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "default_precision_margin_nagelkerke", value = 0.05, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "default_precision_margin_intercept", value = 0.05, unit = "proportion")
  )
)

cat("\n=== JSON OUTPUT ===\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(json_output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))
cat("\n")

plan.estimand: Minimum total development sample size for a binary clinical prediction model meeting Riley precision criteria
plan.hypothesis: The fitted prediction model will achieve adequate shrinkage-adjusted discrimination and calibration precision

parameters.name: Target average outcome-risk absolute margin of error

assumptions: Riley criteria for binary prediction model sample size adequacy
Precision criteria focus on shrinkage-adjusted R-squared difference and calibration
No events-per-variable rule invoked; precision-based calculation governs
Shrinkage factor 0.90 reflects expected optimism correction
Nagelkerke R-squared scale used for binary outcome context
Package default precision implementation (pmsampsize 1.1.3)
scientific_notes: Riley et al. (2018) criteria recommend sample size based on precision of key model parameters and performance metrics
Precision calculation targets the calibration intercept and slope, and discrimination (R-squared) shrinkage
The maximum absolute margin of 0.05 on Nagelkerke scale defines acceptable optimism in the fitted model
Verification step: compute achieved precision at returned N and preceding design to confirm adequacy
Average outcome-risk margin of error 0.05 provides supplementary calibration precision metric

# Install pmsampsize if needed and load it
if (!requireNamespace("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize")
}
library(pmsampsize)

# Confirm package version
packageVersion("pmsampsize")

# Set up parameters for binary prediction model
# Riley criteria for binary outcome (logistic regression)
p <- 24  # candidate predictors (excluding intercept)
prevalence <- 0.174  # event prevalence
rsq_adj <- 0.288  # anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
shrinkage_factor <- 0.90  # expected shrinkage
margin_nagelkerke <- 0.05  # maximum absolute margin (Nagelkerke scale)
confidence <- 0.95  # confidence level for precision
outcome_margin <- 0.05  # target average outcome-risk absolute margin

# Use pmsampsize for binary outcome model
# The function pmsampsize() for type="binary" implements Riley criteria
# Default precision criteria: aim for narrow CI around calibration intercept/slope
# and control shrinkage in R-squared

result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "binary",
  rsquared = rsq_adj,
  parameters = p,
  prevalence = prevalence,
  shrinkage = shrinkage_factor,
  conf.level = confidence,
  margin = margin_nagelkerke  # precision margin on Nagelkerke scale
)

# Display the result object and extract key values
print(result)
cat("\n--- Summary of Results ---\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size:", result$samplesize, "\n")
cat("Minimum events required:", result$events, "\n")

# Verify precision at the returned sample size
# Extract the achieved metrics
achieved_sample_size <- result$samplesize
achieved_events <- result$events
achieved_non_events <- achieved_sample_size - achieved_events

cat("\nVerification at returned sample size (N =", achieved_sample_size, "):\n")
cat("  Events:", achieved_events, "\n")
cat("  Non-events:", achieved_non_events, "\n")
cat("  Prevalence check:", achieved_events / achieved_sample_size, "\n")

# Store results for JSON output
results_list <- list(
  sample_size = achieved_sample_size,
  events = achieved_events,
  non_events = achieved_non_events,
  prevalence_achieved = achieved_events / achieved_sample_size,
  parameters = p,
  rsquared_anticipated = rsq_adj,
  shrinkage_factor = shrinkage_factor,
  margin_nagelkerke = margin_nagelkerke,
  outcome_margin_target = outcome_margin
)

# Output as JSON for structured reporting
library(jsonlite)
output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = achieved_sample_size, unit = "participants_total"),
    list(metric = "minimum_events", value = achieved_events, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "anticipated_adjusted_r_squared", value = rsq_adj, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "shrinkage_factor", value = shrinkage_factor, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "maximum_absolute_margin_nagelkerke", value = margin_nagelkerke, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "achieved_prevalence", value = achieved_events / achieved_sample_size, unit = "proportion")
  )
)

cat("\n--- JSON Output ---\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))
cat("\n")

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

library(pmsampsize)
library(jsonlite)

# Confirm package version
pkg_version <- packageVersion("pmsampsize")
cat("Package version:", as.character(pkg_version), "\n\n")

# Parameters from user request
p <- 24                    # candidate predictors (excluding intercept)
prevalence <- 0.174        # event prevalence
cs_rsquared <- 0.288       # anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
shrinkage_factor <- 0.90   # expected shrinkage
# Note: The user specified "maximum absolute apparent-versus-adjusted R-squared difference 0.05 (Nagelkerke scale)"
# This is the package default, so no need to specify it separately

# Run pmsampsize with binary outcome type
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "b",
  csrsquared = cs_rsquared,
  parameters = p,
  prevalence = prevalence,
  shrinkage = shrinkage_factor
)

# Display detailed results
cat("=== DETAILED OUTPUT ===\n")
print(result)

# Extract key values from the result object
min_sample_size <- result$samplesize
min_events <- result$events
final_shrinkage <- result$shrinkage
final_epp <- result$epp

cat("\n=== EXTRACTION OF KEY RESULTS ===\n")
cat("Minimum sample size (participants_total):", min_sample_size, "\n")
cat("Minimum events:", min_events, "\n")
cat("Achieved shrinkage:", final_shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Events per predictor parameter (EPP):", final_epp, "\n")
cat("Prevalence check: Implied prevalence from N and events:", min_events / min_sample_size, "\n")

# Verify the precision metrics at the returned sample size
# According to Riley criteria, for binary outcomes:
# - Criterion 1: Shrinkage <= 0.9 (actually >=0.9 for inverse direction, shrinkage of effects)
# - Criterion 2: Acceptable difference in apparent vs adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.05
# - Criterion 3: Precision in intercept estimation = 0.05 margin of error

# Calculate the adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared based on Cox-Snell and prevalence
# The relationship is: Nagelkerke = Cox-Snell / (1 - exp(-2*LogL/n)) approximately
# Simplified approach: approximate Nagelkerke R-squared 
prevalence_prob <- prevalence
nag_rsquared <- result$nagrsquared

cat("\n=== NAGELKERKE SCALING AND PRECISION VERIFICATION ===\n")
cat("Cox-Snell R-squared (input):", cs_rsquared, "\n")
cat("Nagelkerke R-squared (from output):", nag_rsquared, "\n")

# The output matrix shows the criteria each applies to
# Extract the criteria results table if available
if (!is.null(result$criteria_results)) {
  cat("\nDetailed Criteria Results:\n")
  print(result$criteria_results)
}

# Prepare JSON output with all computed results
json_output <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = min_sample_size, unit = "participants_total"),
    list(metric = "minimum_events", value = min_events, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "anticipated_adjusted_cox_snell_rsquared", value = cs_rsquared, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "nagelkerke_rsquared", value = nag_rsquared, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "achieved_shrinkage", value = final_shrinkage, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "events_per_predictor_parameter", value = final_epp, unit = "ratio"),
    list(metric = "prevalence", value = prevalence, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "implied_prevalence_at_N", value = min_events / min_sample_size, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "number_candidate_predictors", value = p, unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "default_precision_margin_nagelkerke", value = 0.05, unit = "proportion"),
    list(metric = "default_precision_margin_intercept", value = 0.05, unit = "proportion")
  )
)

cat("\n=== JSON OUTPUT ===\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(json_output, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))
cat("\n")
